name: Product Analytics and Growth for Builders
level: In-depth engineering course · no official exam
audience: Founders and engineers in small teams who own the product numbers: what to measure, how to run experiments and how to grow without a data team.
format: This site's course with a 40-question practice test of metric-design, read-the-query, interpret-the-experiment and pricing questions.

domains.name: Metrics that matter
domains.summary: Choosing what to measure: a north-star metric with a small tree of input metrics, precise activation, retention and revenue definitions, guardrail and counter metrics against Goodhart's law, leading versus lagging indicators and metric windows, and definitions two people compute the same way.

domains.name: Instrumentation and data
domains.summary: Getting trustworthy data: event naming and tracking plans, identity resolution from anonymous to signed-in and account level, client versus server events and ad-blocker loss, consent, cookieless and first-party analytics under GDPR, ePrivacy and UK PECR, and idempotent loads into Postgres or a warehouse.

domains.summary: Running A/B tests that hold up: hypotheses, units of randomisation and MDE, sample size and power computed by hand, confidence intervals, peeking and sequential tests, multiple comparisons, sample ratio mismatch, novelty and bucketing bugs, and feature-flag rollouts when an A/B test is the wrong tool.

lessons.title: North-star and input metrics, metric trees, vanity metrics
lessons.summary: How to pick one north-star metric that captures delivered customer value, break it into a small set of input metrics you can actually move, and recognise vanity metrics that only ever go up.

sections.heading: What a north-star metric is
sections.body:
A north-star metric is a single number that expresses the value customers get from the product, in a way that also predicts the business result. Amplitude's North Star materials illustrate this with a grocery-delivery app. A metric such as "total monthly items received on time" counts value *delivered* (items arrived on time), not activity (app opens) or money (revenue), and it grows only when customers are actually served.

A good north star has three properties:

- **It measures customer value**, so moving it is good for users, not just for a dashboard.
- **It leads revenue.** If it rises, revenue and retention should follow later.
- **The team can influence it** through product work, at least through its inputs.

Revenue itself is a poor north star for most product teams: it lags, it is driven by pricing and sales as much as product, and it says nothing about *why* it moved.

sections.heading: Input metrics and the metric tree
sections.body:
The north star is too slow and too aggregate to steer week-to-week work. You decompose it into **input metrics** that teams own. Amplitude suggests a heuristic of **breadth, depth, frequency and efficiency**, and recommends roughly **3-5 inputs**:

| Lever | Question | Example for a team-docs SaaS |
|---|---|---|
| Breadth | How many accounts get value? | Weekly active workspaces |
| Depth | How much value per account? | Docs edited by 2+ people per workspace |
| Frequency | How often? | Days per week with an edit |
| Efficiency | How fast or easy? | Median time from signup to first shared doc |

Written out, this is a **metric tree**: the north star at the root, inputs beneath it, and below those the specific features or funnels that move each input. A tree makes two things explicit: which team owns which branch, and how a change in a leaf is supposed to flow up. If you cannot draw the arrow from your project to an input metric, the project probably should not be on the roadmap.

sections.heading: Vanity metrics
sections.body:
A vanity metric looks good but does not inform a decision. Typical signs:

- **Cumulative totals** ("1 million signups all time") can only rise, so they never tell you something is wrong.
- **Raw counts without a denominator** (page views, downloads) rise with marketing spend whether or not the product works.
- **Easily gamed activity** (notifications sent, sessions started) can be inflated by the product itself.

The fix is usually to add a denominator, a time window and a value condition: replace "total signups" with "share of this week's signups who reached activation within 7 days". Microsoft ExP's STEDII checklist is a useful filter: a metric should be **sensitive** (it moves when the product changes), **trustworthy**, **efficient** to compute, **debuggable**, **interpretable and actionable**, and **inclusive and fair** across user groups.

sections.heading: Choosing for your product
sections.body: Start from the moment a customer gets value, not from the data you already collect. For a marketplace that might be completed transactions; for a collaboration tool, active collaborative workspaces; for a consumer content app, sessions with meaningful consumption. Then check: would a bad actor or a lazy team be able to raise it without users being better off? If yes, it needs guardrails (see the guardrails lesson) or a better definition.

keyPoints: A north star measures delivered customer value and leads revenue; it is not revenue itself.
Decompose it into roughly 3-5 input metrics along breadth, depth, frequency and efficiency.
A metric tree links each team's work to an input and each input to the north star.
Vanity metrics are cumulative, denominator-free or easily gamed; add a window, a denominator and a value condition.
Use STEDII (sensitive, trustworthy, efficient, debuggable, interpretable/actionable, inclusive) to vet any candidate metric.

gotchas.trap: Use monthly revenue as the product team's north star because the board cares about it.
gotchas.correct: Revenue lags and mixes in pricing and sales effects; pick a value-delivered metric that leads revenue and track revenue as the business outcome.

gotchas.trap: Track 15 "input metrics" so every team has one.
gotchas.correct: Keep it to a handful (Amplitude suggests 3-5) so they stay causal levers, not a dashboard of everything.

gotchas.trap: Report cumulative registered users as growth.
gotchas.correct: Cumulative totals cannot fall; report a windowed rate such as weekly activated new users.

lessons.lab: Pick a product you know. Write its north star in one sentence, then draw a metric tree with one input each for breadth, depth, frequency and efficiency. For each input, name one project that would move it and one way it could be gamed.

lessons.title: AARRR metrics defined precisely
lessons.summary: Acquisition, activation, retention, referral and revenue as concrete, computable metrics for a SaaS or consumer app, with explicit events, populations and time windows.

sections.heading: The funnel as a framework
sections.body: AARRR (acquisition, activation, retention, referral, revenue) is a framework, not a standard: no standards body defines it, so each team must turn each letter into a precise metric. "Activation is up" means nothing until you say *which users*, *which event* and *within what window*.

sections.heading: Acquisition and activation
sections.body:
**Acquisition** counts new people arriving, ideally new *accounts* or *signups* attributed to a channel, measured per period. Raw visits are a weak proxy.

**Activation** is the share of new users who reach a first-value moment within a fixed window after signup. A precise definition looks like:

> Activation rate (week W) = users who signed up in week W **and** performed `doc_shared` with at least one collaborator **within 7 days of signup**, divided by all users who signed up in week W.

The activation event should be one that correlates with later retention; picking "completed onboarding tour" usually measures the tour, not value. The window matters: a funnel tool such as Mixpanel defaults to a 7-day conversion window, but you should choose and state yours explicitly.

sections.heading: Engagement and retention
sections.body:
**Engagement** measures how much and how often active users use the product: DAU/WAU/MAU with a stated *active* definition, the DAU/MAU ratio ("stickiness"), or days active per week. "Active" must be a meaningful event (edited a doc), not just "app opened" or "any event", which background pings can inflate.

**Retention** asks: of a cohort that started in period 0, what share is active in period N? The bucket definition changes the answer:

- **N-day (Mixpanel "On")**: active in exactly that bucket.
- **Unbounded (Amplitude also calls it rolling; Mixpanel "On or After", the default)**: active in that bucket *or any later one*. This is always at least as high as N-day.
- **Bracket (Amplitude)**: custom windows such as days 0-5, 6-13.

Separately, Mixpanel's rolling time-window mode (its default) measures Day 1 as 24-48 hours after the cohort event and Week 1 as days 7-14; calendar mode uses calendar days instead. Always state which you use.

sections.heading: Referral and revenue
sections.body:
**Referral** is usually invites sent per active user and the conversion rate of those invites into new activated users; their product is a viral coefficient. Define both halves with windows.

**Revenue** metrics for subscriptions include MRR, conversion from free to paid within N days, ARPA (average revenue per account) and net and gross revenue retention. Revenue is the most lagging of the five; it is the outcome, while activation and retention are the levers.

sections.heading: SaaS vs consumer
sections.body: In B2B SaaS the unit of value is often the **account (workspace)**, not the user: an account with one heavy user and nine idle seats behaves differently from ten light users. Define activation and retention at the account level as well as the user level. In consumer apps the user is the unit, and frequency expectations differ: a ride app may expect weekly use, a tax app yearly. Choose the retention bucket to match the natural usage frequency.

keyPoints: AARRR is a framework; each letter must be made into a metric with a population, an event and a window.
Activation = share of a signup cohort reaching a value event within a fixed window after signup.
"Active" must be a meaningful action, not any event or an app open.
Unbounded ("On or After") retention is always at least as high as N-day ("On") retention for the same cohort.
For B2B, measure at the account level too; match retention buckets to natural usage frequency.

gotchas.trap: Compare an unbounded retention curve from one tool with an N-day curve from another.
gotchas.correct: Confirm both use the same bucket definition (N-day vs unbounded, rolling vs calendar) before comparing.

gotchas.trap: Define activation as "completed onboarding".
gotchas.correct: Pick an event that reflects first value and correlates with later retention, measured within a stated window.

gotchas.trap: Count any tracked event as "active".
gotchas.correct: Background or automatic events inflate DAU; define active as a user-initiated value action.

lessons.lab: Write one-line definitions for activation, weekly active user, Week-4 retention (both N-day and unbounded) and free-to-paid conversion for a product you know. Each must name the population, the qualifying event, the time zone and the window.

lessons.title: Guardrail and counter metrics; Goodhart's law
lessons.summary: Why every target metric needs counter metrics, how Microsoft ExP separates data-quality, goal and guardrail metrics, and how Goodhart's law shows up in product teams.

sections.heading: Goodhart's law
sections.body:
The usual paraphrase of Goodhart's law: *when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.* Once a team is rewarded for moving a number, it will find the cheapest way to move it, and the cheapest way often breaks the link between the number and real value. Examples:

- Target "notifications opened" and the team sends more notifications; opens rise, uninstalls rise too.
- Target "time in app" and the team adds friction; users spend longer but accomplish less.
- Target "signups" and the team removes email verification; signups rise, spam accounts rise.

sections.heading: Three kinds of metric
sections.body:
Microsoft's Experimentation Platform (ExP) separates metrics into:

1. **Data-quality metrics**: is the data trustworthy? Examples are sample ratio mismatch (SRM), data loss and join rates. They decide whether the rest can be trusted, so check them *first*; an SRM typically invalidates the test.
2. **OEC (overall evaluation criterion) metrics**: the goal you are trying to move.
3. **Guardrail metrics**: things that should *not* get worse, such as page load time, crash rate or abandonment.

The KDD 2017 "Dirty Dozen" pitfalls paper makes the same point: check data-quality metrics before interpreting the OEC, and keep guardrails separate from the goal.

sections.heading: Counter metrics
sections.body:
A **counter metric** is paired with a specific target to catch the obvious way of gaming it. It is narrower than a general guardrail:

| Target | Counter metric |
|---|---|
| Notification open rate | Notification opt-out / uninstall rate |
| Support tickets closed per agent | Ticket reopen rate, CSAT |
| Trial signups | Activation rate of those signups |
| Checkout conversion | Refund and chargeback rate |

Write the counter metric down at the same time as the target and review them together. A win on the target with a loss on its counter is not a win.

sections.heading: Guardrails in practice
sections.body: Guardrails are usually **platform-wide** and shared: performance (load time, error rate), business health (revenue, unsubscribes) and trust (crash rate, complaint rate). They are evaluated on every launch or experiment with a pre-agreed tolerance, for example "no statistically significant increase in crash rate". Agree tolerances before the result is known; deciding afterwards invites motivated reasoning.

keyPoints: When a measure becomes a target it tends to stop measuring what you wanted (Goodhart).
ExP separates data-quality, OEC (goal) and guardrail metrics; check data quality first.
Pair each target with a counter metric that catches its most likely gaming.
Guardrails such as latency, crash rate and abandonment should not degrade; set tolerances in advance.

gotchas.trap: Read the OEC first and look at data-quality checks only if the result looks odd.
gotchas.correct: Check data-quality metrics (such as SRM) first; a failed check invalidates the OEC result whatever it says.

gotchas.trap: Fold guardrails into a single weighted score with the goal.
gotchas.correct: Keep guardrails separate so a goal win cannot hide a guardrail regression.

gotchas.trap: Choose counter metrics after the launch, once you see what moved.
gotchas.correct: Define counters alongside the target before the work starts.

lessons.lab: Take one team goal you have seen (for example "increase weekly notifications opened by 10%"). Write the cheapest way to hit it that hurts users, then the counter metric that would catch it, and one platform guardrail with a tolerance.

lessons.title: Leading vs lagging indicators and metric windows
lessons.summary: How to use fast leading metrics to steer without being fooled by short-term effects, and how the choice of window (attribution, conversion, retention bucket, rolling vs calendar) changes the number.

sections.heading: Leading and lagging
sections.body:
A **lagging indicator** reports an outcome after the fact: revenue, annual churn, renewals. It is what you ultimately care about but it moves slowly and has many causes. A **leading indicator** moves earlier and predicts the lagging one: activation rate, week-1 retention, depth of first-week use.

The ExP pitfalls paper notes that the OEC used in experiments is usually a leading metric, precisely because the true outcome takes too long to observe. The risk is that the link between leading and lagging is assumed rather than checked.

sections.heading: When short-term metrics mislead
sections.body:
Google's KDD 2015 study on ads blindness (Hohnhold, O'Brien and Tang) found that user learning in response to a change "takes a long time to converge": showing more ads lifted short-term revenue, while users gradually learned to ignore or avoid ads, so the long-term effect differed. Lessons for product teams:

- **Novelty effects** inflate early engagement with anything new; it fades.
- **Learning effects** can go either way and take weeks to settle.
- Validate a leading metric against the lagging one using past cohorts, and hold out a long-running control for big changes where you can.

sections.heading: Windows change the number
sections.body:
Every rate needs a window, and each choice changes the answer:

- **Conversion window**: "converted within 7 days" vs "within 30 days". Longer windows give higher rates and slower readouts.
- **Retention bucket**: N-day ("On") vs unbounded ("On or After"); rolling (Day 1 = 24-48 h after the start event in Mixpanel) vs calendar days.
- **Active window**: daily vs weekly vs monthly active, and the ratio between them.
- **Cohort maturity**: a cohort that started 10 days ago cannot have a Day-30 value yet. Exclude immature cohorts rather than reading them as zero.

sections.heading: Choosing a window
sections.body: Match the window to how often a user naturally gets value. A daily-use messaging app can use Day-1 and Day-7 retention; a monthly-billing tool needs weekly or monthly buckets. Then pick the **shortest window that still predicts the lagging outcome**, so you get fast feedback without measuring noise. Write the choice into the metric definition so a later analyst does not silently change it.

keyPoints: Lagging metrics (revenue, churn) are the outcome; leading metrics (activation, early retention) steer.
Experiment OECs are usually leading metrics, so validate their link to the outcome.
Short-term effects can differ from long-term ones (novelty, user learning); Google's ads-blindness study is the classic example.
Conversion windows, retention buckets and rolling vs calendar modes all change the value; state them.
Exclude immature cohorts instead of treating missing periods as zero.

gotchas.trap: Declare a feature a success because week-1 engagement jumped.
gotchas.correct: Check for novelty: compare later weeks and confirm the leading metric predicts the outcome.

gotchas.trap: Show the latest cohort with a 0% Day-30 value on the retention chart.
gotchas.correct: That cohort has not reached Day 30; exclude or mark it as incomplete.

gotchas.trap: Pick a 30-day conversion window for a weekly product to get bigger numbers.
gotchas.correct: Choose the shortest window that still predicts the outcome and match it to natural usage frequency.

lessons.lab: Take past signup cohorts and compute week-1 activation and month-3 retention for each. Check whether the cohorts with higher activation also retained better. If they did not, your activation definition is not a good leading indicator.

lessons.title: Writing metric definitions people can compute the same way twice
lessons.summary: A template for metric definitions that removes ambiguity: population, qualifying events, identity, time zone, window, filters, numerator and denominator, and owner.

sections.heading: Why definitions drift
sections.body: Two analysts asked for "weekly active users" will often return different numbers. Common reasons: one counts devices and the other users; one uses UTC and the other local time; one excludes internal and test accounts; one counts any event and the other a value event; one uses calendar weeks and the other rolling 7 days. None is wrong, but a metric that can be computed two ways cannot be trusted or compared over time.

sections.heading: A definition template
sections.body:
A complete metric definition states:

| Field | Example |
|---|---|
| Name | `weekly_active_workspaces` |
| Question it answers | How many workspaces got value this week? |
| Unit of analysis | Workspace (account), not user or device |
| Qualifying event(s) | `doc_edited` by a non-bot member, exact event names |
| Numerator / denominator | Count of distinct workspaces with 1+ qualifying event (no denominator; a count) |
| Window | ISO calendar week, Monday 00:00 to Sunday 23:59 **UTC** |
| Filters | Exclude internal domains, test workspaces, suspended accounts |
| Identity rule | Events attributed by `workspace_id` on the event |
| Late data | Recompute the last 3 days on each run |
| Source of truth | Table or SQL view name, versioned |
| Owner | Growth analytics |

The most valuable field is often the reference SQL: the definition *is* the query, kept in version control.

sections.heading: Event names that support definitions
sections.body: Definitions are only as stable as the events beneath them. Mixpanel's guidance is to use consistent snake_case names in an object-verb form (for example `song_played`), remembering names are case-sensitive, and to never put dynamic values in event names; put them in properties instead. `Signup`, `signup` and `sign_up` are three different events to the tool, and a metric that counts one of them will silently miss the others.

sections.heading: Change control
sections.body: When a definition must change, version it (`wau_v2`), backfill both versions for an overlap period, and annotate dashboards with the change date. Silent redefinition is how year-over-year charts end up comparing two different metrics. Microsoft ExP's STEDII "trustworthy" and "debuggable" properties apply here: a metric you cannot recompute and trace back to raw events cannot be debugged.

keyPoints: Ambiguity usually comes from unit of analysis, time zone, window, filters and qualifying events.
Write a definition with name, question, unit, events, numerator/denominator, window, filters, identity rule, source and owner.
Keep the reference query in version control; the query is the definition.
Use consistent, case-sensitive snake_case object-verb event names with dynamic values in properties.
Version and annotate definition changes instead of redefining silently.

gotchas.trap: Define WAU as "users active this week".
gotchas.correct: State the unit, the qualifying event, the week boundary and time zone, and exclusions.

gotchas.trap: Include the plan name in the event name, e.g. `upgraded_to_pro`.
gotchas.correct: Use one event (`plan_upgraded`) with the plan as a property.

gotchas.trap: Change the activation event and keep the old chart title.
gotchas.correct: Version the metric, backfill for overlap and annotate the change.

lessons.lab: Write a full definition for "Week-4 retention of new workspaces" using the template. Give it to a colleague with raw event data and ask them to compute it independently; reconcile every difference by tightening the definition.

lessons.title: Event design and tracking plans
lessons.summary: Good analytics starts with a small, consistent event vocabulary, typed properties and a tracking plan that a schema check enforces.

sections.heading: Name events like a public API
sections.body:
An event name is a contract. Dashboards, funnels and alerts all depend on it, so renaming one later breaks history.

Mixpanel's guidance is a good default for any tool:

- **Object + verb, past tense, snake_case:** `song_played`, `signup_completed`, `invoice_paid`.
- **Names are case-sensitive.** `Signup_Completed` and `signup_completed` are two different events.
- **Never put dynamic values in the name.** Use `plan_upgraded` with a `plan` property, not `plan_upgraded_to_pro_annual`.

| Bad | Why | Better |
|---|---|---|
| `Clicked Signup Button - Pricing Page` | UI wording plus location baked into the name | `signup_started` + `source_page: "pricing"` |
| `search_for_running_shoes` | Dynamic value in the name; endless distinct names | `search_performed` + `query_length` |
| `purchase` and `Purchase` | Case drift splits one event in two | one canonical `order_completed` |

Track **meaningful state changes** (signup completed, project created, invite accepted), not every click. Twenty well-defined events beat four hundred vague ones.

sections.heading: Properties, identities and limits
sections.body:
Each event carries three kinds of context:

- **Event properties:** facts about this occurrence (`plan`, `amount_cents`, `source_page`).
- **User properties:** facts about the person that change slowly (`signup_cohort`, `role`).
- **Identity and group keys:** who did it (anonymous or user ID) and which account it belongs to (see the identity lesson).

Give each property **one type and one unit**, and encode the unit in the name (`amount_cents`, `duration_ms`). Mixed types (`"12"` in some events, `12` in others) quietly break breakdowns.

Tools enforce limits, and they truncate rather than fail loudly. At the time of writing:

| Tool | Notable limits |
|---|---|
| Mixpanel | 255 properties per event; names and values truncated at 255 characters; events under 1 MB; soft limit of 5,000 distinct event names |
| GA4 | event names 40 characters; 25 parameters per event; most parameter values 100 characters; 25 user properties |

Check the current limits pages before you design around a number. The design lesson is stable: short names, a bounded set of events, and IDs instead of long free text.

sections.heading: The tracking plan
sections.body:
A **tracking plan** is the single source of truth for what is tracked. Keep it in the repo (YAML or JSON) so changes go through code review.

| Column | Example |
|---|---|
| Event | `project_created` |
| Trigger (exact moment) | After the API returns 201, not on button click |
| Properties, type, required | `template: string?`, `is_first_project: boolean` |
| Source | server |
| Owner | growth team |
| Question it answers | Activation: % of signups who create a project in 24 h |

The **trigger** column matters most. "When the user creates a project" is ambiguous. Does it fire on click, on success or on retry? Two engineers will implement it differently, and the numbers will disagree.

Every event should map to a question or metric. If nobody can name the decision an event informs, don't add it.

sections.heading: Schema validation and versioning
sections.body:
A plan nobody enforces drifts within weeks. Enforce it in three places:

1. **Typed wrapper.** Generate a `track()` function from the plan, so `track('project_created', {...})` fails type-checking when a property is missing or misspelled. A runtime schema library such as Zod can validate the payload too.
2. **CI.** Fail the build if code calls an event that is not in the plan.
3. **Ingest.** Validate again server-side and **quarantine** invalid events in a separate table with the error, instead of silently dropping them. Silent drops look exactly like a real decline.

```ts
const ProjectCreated = z.object({
  template: z.string().optional(),
  is_first_project: z.boolean(),
});
```

**Versioning:** adding an optional property is safe. Changing a property's meaning or type is a breaking change, so ship a new event name (or a `schema_version` property) and keep the old one until dashboards move over. Annotate dashboards on the day you ship it.

keyPoints: Use object_verb snake_case names; names are case-sensitive.
Put variable values in properties, never in event names.
Write the exact trigger moment for every event in a versioned tracking plan.
Validate in the type system, in CI and at ingest; quarantine bad events rather than dropping them.
Analytics tools truncate over-limit names and values, so design short names and bounded vocabularies.

gotchas.trap: Naming events after UI copy (`Clicked Blue Button`).
gotchas.correct: Name the user outcome (`checkout_started`), so a redesign does not rename the metric.

gotchas.trap: Firing "created" events on click, before the server confirms.
gotchas.correct: Fire success events after the server confirms, ideally from the server.

gotchas.trap: Silently dropping events that fail validation.
gotchas.correct: Quarantine them with the error so a drop in counts can be diagnosed.

lessons.lab: Write a tracking plan in YAML for a signup → first project → invite funnel (5-7 events). For each event give the trigger, typed properties and source. Then write a Zod schema for two of the events and a tiny script that rejects a payload with a misspelled property.

lessons.title: Identity resolution and account analytics
lessons.summary: Join anonymous visits to signed-in users without merging different people, and model B2B accounts as groups.

sections.heading: Anonymous, identified and merged
sections.body:
Every analytics SDK starts a visitor as **anonymous**, with a random device or anonymous ID stored on the device. When the person signs up or logs in, you call **identify** with your own user ID. The tool then links the anonymous history to that user:

- **PostHog:** `identify` merges the anonymous person into the identified person, so pre-signup events belong to the user.
- **Mixpanel (Simplified ID Merge):** `$device_id` and `$user_id` form an identity cluster. The canonical `distinct_id` becomes the `$user_id`, and the merge is **retroactive**.
- **Amplitude:** a device ID plus a user ID resolve to one Amplitude ID.

Call identify **at signup and at every login**, as early as you know the ID. Calling it on login is what joins a second device.

sections.heading: Choosing the user ID
sections.body:
Use a **stable, internal, opaque ID**, usually your database primary key or a UUID.

- **Not email.** Emails change, and Amplitude explicitly warns against IDs that change. An email is also personal data that you then copy into every event.
- **IDs are case-sensitive** (Amplitude), so `User_42` and `user_42` are two people. Normalise once.
- **Never a placeholder.** Sending `"guest"`, `"null"` or `"0"` as an ID merges every anonymous visitor into one giant fake user. PostHog rejects IDs such as `anonymous`, `guest`, `null`, `undefined` and `0`. Amplitude warns against strings like `None`. If you don't have a real ID, don't call identify.

sections.heading: Logout, shared devices and merge limits
sections.body:
- **Call `reset()` on logout** (PostHog, Mixpanel, Amplitude). It clears the user ID and starts a new anonymous ID. Without it, the next person on a shared laptop is recorded as the previous user.
- **Two identified users cannot be merged into one.** PostHog cannot identify an already-identified user as a different ID. Mixpanel cannot merge two `$user_id`s. This guard stops one shared device from fusing two real accounts.
- **Alias and forced merge.** PostHog's `alias` adds a second ID to a person. `$merge_dangerously` merges two identified persons and is **irreversible**, so use it only when you are certain they are the same human.
- Mixpanel's legacy `alias()` was not retroactive. The simplified model replaced it.

sections.heading: Cross-device journeys
sections.body:
A person who browses on a phone and buys on a laptop is two anonymous IDs until they log in on both. After identify runs on each device with the **same user ID**, both histories join that user.

What you still can't see: anonymous sessions on a device where they never log in. Expect "new visitor" counts to be inflated and treat pre-login attribution as approximate.

Don't fingerprint devices to fill the gap. It is unreliable, and in the EU it falls under the same consent rules as cookies (see the privacy lesson).

sections.heading: Accounts as groups
sections.body:
B2B products are bought by accounts, not people. "Weekly active **accounts**" needs events tied to a company.

- **PostHog group analytics:** up to **5 group types** per project (e.g. `company`, `workspace`). An event can belong to only one group of each type. Group membership lives **on events**, not on persons, so you must attach the group to each event, typically by calling `group()` after login.
- Keep a stable account ID, just like the user ID. Don't use the company name.
- A user in two workspaces is normal. Because membership is per event, each event counts toward the workspace it happened in.

**Cost note:** PostHog's `person_profiles` default is `identified_only`, and anonymous events are "up to 4x cheaper". Not every marketing-page view needs a person profile.

keyPoints: Identify at signup and every login with a stable internal ID.
Never use email, changing values or placeholder strings as the user ID.
Call reset() on logout so shared devices do not mix people.
Tools refuse to merge two identified users; forced merges are irreversible.
Attach a group (account) key to events for B2B metrics; membership is per event.

gotchas.trap: Using email as the distinct ID because it is human-readable.
gotchas.correct: Use the database ID; store email (if at all) as a user property in your own systems.

gotchas.trap: Calling identify("guest") for logged-out users.
gotchas.correct: Stay anonymous until there is a real ID; placeholders merge everyone into one user.

gotchas.trap: Expecting user properties to give account-level metrics.
gotchas.correct: Use group analytics, and attach the group key to each event.

lessons.lab: In a small app with PostHog or Mixpanel in dev mode, browse anonymously, sign up, log out, then log in as a second user in the same browser. Verify in the live events view that pre-signup events joined user 1 and that user 2 is separate. Then remove the reset() call and repeat to see the contamination.

lessons.title: Client vs server events and data loss
lessons.summary: Decide where each event is captured, measure how much you lose to ad blockers and page unloads, and sample without breaking funnels.

sections.heading: Where each event should come from
sections.body:
| Capture on the client | Capture on the server |
|---|---|
| UI interactions with no backend call (opened a modal, viewed a tab) | Business outcomes: `signup_completed`, `order_completed`, `invoice_paid` |
| Page views and session context (referrer, viewport) | Events with no browser present: renewals, webhooks, background jobs |
| Client performance (load times) | Anything you will reconcile against money or a database |

**Rule of thumb:** if the event changes a row in your database, emit it from the server right after the change commits. Server events are not affected by ad blockers, closed tabs or flaky mobile networks, and they reflect what actually happened, not what the UI attempted.

Pass the same user ID (and, if you have it, the anonymous ID from the client) to the server event so identity resolution still works.

sections.heading: Ad blockers and reverse proxies
sections.body:
Browser privacy extensions commonly block requests to known analytics hosts. Client-side counts are then **systematically low**, and the bias is not random: technical audiences block more.

- A **reverse proxy** serves the analytics endpoint from your own domain. PostHog says this "typically increases event capture by 10-30%". Its managed proxy is free on PostHog Cloud, but PostHog notes it is not HIPAA-compliant.
- A proxy fixes delivery, **not consent**. If a user has refused analytics, you still must not track them (see the privacy lesson).
- For conversions that matter, server-side capture removes the gap entirely.

sections.heading: Measuring data loss
sections.body:
Microsoft's ExP team treats **data-quality metrics** (such as data loss and join rates) as a separate class of metric that you check before trusting anything else. Do the same:

- **Reconcile daily:** analytics `signup_completed` count vs `SELECT count(*) FROM users WHERE created_at::date = ...`. Alert when the gap moves.
- **Page unload loss:** events fired as the user navigates away are often cancelled. `navigator.sendBeacon()` queues a small POST that the browser delivers even as the page unloads. Most SDKs batch and use it, or something like it, for you.
- **Mobile:** SDKs queue events offline and flush later, so events arrive late. Analyse by event time, not arrival time.
- **Duplicates:** retries can double-send. Give each event a client-generated UUID and deduplicate on it (see the warehouse lesson).

sections.heading: Sampling without breaking funnels
sections.body:
Sampling cuts cost, but **how** you sample decides what still works.

- **Per-event random sampling** keeps 10% of events independently. A user's signup survives but their activation does not, so funnels and retention become nonsense.
- **Per-user deterministic sampling** keeps 100% of events for 10% of users. Hash the user (or anonymous) ID into [0,1] and keep the user if the hash is below the rate. This is the same technique feature-flag systems use for stable bucketing (PostHog hashes the flag key plus the distinct ID).
- Record the **sample rate** on each event and scale counts by 1/rate.
- Never sample revenue or other server-side business events. They are cheap and they are your ground truth.

Exports can also impose caps. For example, GA4's standard daily BigQuery export has a daily event limit, while streaming export has no event limit but is best-effort. Know the limits of your pipeline before you trust totals.

keyPoints: Emit business outcomes from the server after the database commit.
Ad blockers bias client counts low and non-randomly; a reverse proxy helps delivery but never overrides consent.
Reconcile analytics counts against the database as a data-quality metric.
Sample by user with a deterministic hash, never by event.
Use client-generated event IDs so retries can be deduplicated.

gotchas.trap: Using a reverse proxy to track users who rejected analytics.
gotchas.correct: A proxy changes the host, not the law; consent still applies.

gotchas.trap: Sampling 10% of events at random to save cost.
gotchas.correct: Sample 10% of users by hashed ID so each kept journey is complete.

gotchas.trap: Reading a 15% drop in client signups as a product problem.
gotchas.correct: First compare with the database count; it may be a blocker or SDK release.

lessons.lab: Take a week of your app's signups. Count them in the database and in your analytics tool, and compute the daily loss rate. Then move `signup_completed` to a server-side capture and re-run the comparison for a few days.

lessons.title: Privacy by design for product analytics
lessons.summary: Consent rules for analytics storage in the EU and UK, cookieless options, and how to minimise, retain and delete analytics data.

sections.heading: EU: consent before non-essential storage
sections.body:
**ePrivacy Directive Art. 5(3)** requires consent before storing or reading information on a user's device, unless it is strictly necessary for a service the user requested. Analytics is not strictly necessary, so in the EU **analytics cookies need prior consent**.

- Art. 5(3) applies to the device access itself, **whether or not the data is personal**.
- **EDPB Guidelines 2/2023** (final version adopted October 2024) explain that the article reaches beyond cookies, to techniques such as tracking pixels and URL-based tracking. "We use local storage, not cookies" is not an exemption.
- **Planet49 (CJEU, C-673/17):** pre-ticked boxes are not valid consent, and users must be told how long cookies last and whether third parties can access them.
- The **EDPB Cookie Banner Taskforce** found that most authorities treat a banner with no reject option on any layer as an infringement.

**Status check (late 2026):** the EU Digital Omnibus proposal on cookie rules is not law. Teach and build for the current Art. 5(3) rule.

sections.heading: UK: the statistical-purposes exception
Cookieless and consent-aware setups
sections.body:
You can keep measuring when people decline, at reduced fidelity:

- **PostHog `cookieless_mode`** (`'always'` or `'on_reject'`) sets no cookies and no local or session storage. It must also be enabled in the project settings, or events are ignored. It counts people using a server-side hash with a **daily rotating salt**, so a non-consenting user looks like a **new person each day**. Daily uniques work. Retention and multi-day funnels for those users do not.
- **PostHog persistence:** the default is `localStorage+cookie`. A `memory` setting stores nothing until you switch after consent.
- **Google consent mode:** in **Basic** mode, tags are blocked until consent. In **Advanced** mode, cookieless pings are sent while consent is denied and are used for modelling.

Cookieless is a design choice, not a legal blanket. Get the specific setup reviewed for the markets you serve.

sections.heading: Minimise what you collect
sections.body:
**GDPR Art. 5(1)(c), data minimisation:** collect only what is adequate, relevant and necessary. **Art. 25** asks for data protection by design and by default. In practice:

- Send an **opaque user ID**, not email, name or phone. Join to PII inside your own database only when you need to.
- **Pseudonymous is still personal data** under GDPR, because the ID can be linked back to a person. Minimisation reduces risk but doesn't take the data out of scope.
- Strip query strings and free-text fields that may carry PII (`?email=`, search boxes, support messages) before sending.
- Prefer **booleans and buckets** to raw values: `has_team: true`, `seats_bucket: "6-20"`.
- Know your lawful basis (Art. 6) for each purpose, separately from the ePrivacy consent question.

sections.heading: Retention and deletion
sections.body:
- **Storage limitation (Art. 5(1)(e)):** keep identifiable data no longer than needed. Choose a retention period per table and enforce it with a job, for example by dropping old partitions.
- **Tool settings:** GA4 user- and event-level retention is 2 or 14 months on standard properties. It affects **explorations and funnel reports only**, not standard aggregated reports.
- **Erasure (Art. 17):** a deletion request must reach every copy: the app database, the analytics tool, the warehouse, exports and backups by policy. Keep a written list of where analytics data flows so you can do this in hours, not weeks.
- Aggregates with no way back to the person (daily counts) can usually stay after the raw rows go.

keyPoints: EU: analytics storage or access needs prior consent under ePrivacy Art. 5(3); pixels and local storage count too.
No pre-ticked boxes; always offer a genuine way to reject.
UK: the DUAA statistical exception applies only with aggregate, processor-run, non-advertising analytics plus an easy objection.
Cookieless hashing with a daily salt keeps daily counts but loses multi-day retention for those users.
Send opaque IDs, not PII; pseudonymous data is still personal data.
Map every copy of analytics data so retention and erasure can be enforced.

gotchas.trap: "We use localStorage, not cookies, so no consent is needed."
gotchas.correct: Art. 5(3) covers storing or accessing information on the device, not just cookies.

gotchas.trap: Applying the UK analytics exception to EU visitors.
gotchas.correct: The exception is UK law; EU visitors still need consent for non-essential analytics.

gotchas.trap: Hashing emails and calling the result anonymous.
gotchas.correct: A hash that can be linked back is pseudonymous, which is still personal data.

lessons.lab: Audit your app's analytics calls for one week of events: list every property, mark any that could hold PII, and remove or bucket them. Then configure your SDK so that before consent it stores nothing (memory persistence or a cookieless mode) and confirm in the browser devtools Application tab that no analytics storage is written before you click Accept.

lessons.title: A small-team event warehouse in Postgres
lessons.summary: A single Postgres events table, loaded idempotently and partitioned by time, answers most product questions before you need a dedicated warehouse.

sections.heading: Start with Postgres
sections.body:
For a small product, a dedicated warehouse is often premature. Postgres can handle a large events table with sensible indexes and partitioning, and your analysts already know SQL. Move to a columnar warehouse when scans get slow or analytics load hurts the production database. Before then, a read replica or a separate analytics database is the usual step.

```sql
CREATE TABLE events (
  event_id     uuid        NOT NULL,
  event_name   text        NOT NULL,
  user_id      text,
  anon_id      text,
  account_id   text,
  occurred_at  timestamptz NOT NULL,
  received_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  properties   jsonb       NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
  PRIMARY KEY (event_id, occurred_at)
) PARTITION BY RANGE (occurred_at);
```

Promote properties you filter on constantly into real columns. Leave the long tail in `jsonb`.

sections.heading: Idempotent loads
sections.body:
Pipelines retry, so every load must be safe to run twice.

1. The **client generates `event_id`** (a UUID) when the event happens. A retry sends the same ID.
2. A **unique constraint** covers that ID.
3. Load with `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`:

```sql
INSERT INTO events (event_id, event_name, user_id, occurred_at, properties)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4, $5)
ON CONFLICT (event_id, occurred_at) DO NOTHING;
```

`ON CONFLICT` needs a unique index or constraint that matches the conflict target. Without one, duplicates go straight in. A server-assigned ID (a `serial`, or a UUID created at insert time) cannot deduplicate, because each retry gets a fresh one.

For batch loads from a tool's export, load into a staging table, then insert-select with the same `ON CONFLICT` clause, so re-running a day's file changes nothing.

sections.heading: Two timestamps
sections.body:
Store both:

- **`occurred_at`:** when it happened on the device or server. Analyse with this.
- **`received_at`:** when you ingested it. Use it for pipeline monitoring and for spotting clock skew.

Use `timestamptz`, which stores an absolute instant, and decide on purpose which time zone a "day" means in reports. Mobile events can arrive hours or days late, so a dashboard for "yesterday" may still change. Recompute recent days rather than appending once.

sections.heading: Partitioning and retention
sections.body:
Range-partition by month on `occurred_at`:

- Queries for a date range touch only the matching partitions.
- **Retention is a cheap `DROP TABLE`** (or `DETACH PARTITION`) of the oldest partition, instead of a huge `DELETE` that bloats the table.
- On a partitioned table, Postgres requires unique and primary-key constraints to **include the partition key columns**. That is why the key above is `(event_id, occurred_at)`. It works because a retry resends the same client-set `occurred_at`.

Index what you filter on, e.g. `(event_name, occurred_at)` and `(user_id, occurred_at)`.

sections.heading: Raw, then modelled
sections.body:
Keep the raw events table **append-only**, and build derived tables on top: daily active users, signup funnels, account activity. A **materialized view** (refreshed on a schedule) is the simplest version in Postgres.

When a definition changes, you rebuild the derived table from raw events. You never patch numbers in place, and the old definition stays reproducible from version control.

keyPoints: A Postgres events table with jsonb properties is enough for most early products.
Make loads idempotent with client-generated event IDs plus a unique constraint and ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING.
Store occurred_at and received_at as timestamptz; analyse by occurred_at.
Partition by month; drop partitions for retention.
Keep raw events immutable and rebuild derived tables from them.

gotchas.trap: Deduplicating on a server-generated serial ID.
gotchas.correct: Retries get new serials; deduplicate on an ID generated where the event happened.

gotchas.trap: Expecting ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING to work with no unique constraint.
gotchas.correct: It needs a unique index or constraint that matches the conflict target.

gotchas.trap: Running analytics queries on the primary production database at peak.
gotchas.correct: Use a replica or separate analytics database once queries get heavy.

lessons.title: Funnels in SQL: step order and conversion windows
lessons.summary: How to write a funnel query that respects step order and a conversion window, avoids join fan-out, and handles entrants whose window has not closed yet.

sections.heading: What a funnel query has to decide
sections.body:
A funnel is not "count of people who did A" next to "count of people who did B". Before writing SQL you must fix four things:

1. **Entry**: which event puts a user in the funnel, and in which date range.
2. **Order**: must step 2 happen *after* step 1, or does any order count?
3. **Window**: how long after entry may a user still convert? (A 7-day funnel and a 30-day funnel are different metrics.)
4. **Unit**: are you counting unique users, total attempts, or sessions?

Analytics tools expose the same choices. Mixpanel's funnel report, for example, defaults to a **7-day conversion window** (configurable up to 366 days or 12 sessions), **Specific Order** by default (with Any Order as the alternative), and lets you count **Uniques, Totals or Sessions**. If your SQL and a tool disagree, check these settings first.

sections.heading: Anchor every step to the previous one
sections.body:
The safe pattern is: find each entrant's step-1 time, then look for step 2 **after** that time and **within** the window, then step 3 after step 2, and so on. Aggregate to one row per user *before* joining the next step so a user with many events cannot multiply rows.

~~~sql
WITH s1 AS (
  SELECT user_id, min(ts) AS t1
  FROM events
  WHERE event = 'signup_started'
    AND ts >= '2026-10-01' AND ts < '2026-11-01'
  GROUP BY user_id
), s2 AS (
  SELECT s1.user_id, s1.t1, min(e.ts) AS t2
  FROM s1
  LEFT JOIN events e
    ON e.user_id = s1.user_id
   AND e.event = 'signup_completed'
   AND e.ts > s1.t1
   AND e.ts <= s1.t1 + interval '7 days'
  GROUP BY s1.user_id, s1.t1
), s3 AS (
  SELECT s2.user_id, s2.t2, min(e.ts) AS t3
  FROM s2
  LEFT JOIN events e
    ON e.user_id = s2.user_id
   AND e.event = 'first_project_created'
   AND e.ts > s2.t2
   AND e.ts <= s2.t1 + interval '7 days'
  GROUP BY s2.user_id, s2.t2
)
SELECT count(*) AS started,
       count(t2) AS completed,
       count(t3) AS created_project
FROM s2 JOIN s3 USING (user_id);
~~~

`LEFT JOIN` keeps non-converters, `count(t2)` counts only non-NULL times, and because step 3 joins on `e.ts > s2.t2`, a user with NULL `t2` can never reach step 3. In this pattern the window is anchored at step 1 (`s2.t1 + interval '7 days'`), so the whole funnel must finish within 7 days of entry.

sections.heading: The three classic bugs
sections.body:
- **Unordered steps.** Counting "users who purchased in October" as step 2 includes customers who purchased *before* they ever started signup, or who were already customers. Conversion is inflated and can even exceed 100% for a segment.
- **Fan-out.** Joining raw step-1 events to raw step-2 events on `user_id` produces one row per *pair*. `count(*)` then counts pairs, not people. Aggregate per user first, or count `DISTINCT user_id`.
- **Open windows.** Users who entered yesterday have had one day of a seven-day window. Including them drags conversion down for the most recent period. Either restrict entrants to `t1 <= now() - interval '7 days'` or label the latest period as incomplete.

sections.heading: Denominators and step-to-step rates
sections.body:
Report both **overall conversion** (last step / entrants) and **step conversion** (each step / previous step). The overall number answers "is the funnel getting better?". Step rates show *where* people leave. Always print the entrant count next to the rate: 50% of 12 users is not the same evidence as 50% of 12,000.

When counting Totals instead of Uniques, one determined user who retries checkout ten times counts ten times. That is useful for diagnosing errors and misleading for "what share of people convert".

keyPoints: Decide entry event, step order, conversion window and counting unit before writing SQL.
Find each user's step-1 time, then require each later step to be after the previous step and inside the window.
Aggregate to one row per user before joining the next step to avoid fan-out.
Exclude or label entrants whose conversion window has not closed yet.
Mixpanel funnels default to a 7-day window and Specific Order; check tool settings when numbers disagree.

gotchas.trap: Dividing "users who did step 2 this month" by "users who did step 1 this month".
gotchas.correct: Count only step-1 entrants who then did step 2 after their step-1 time and inside the window.

gotchas.trap: Joining raw event rows of two steps and using count(*).
gotchas.correct: Reduce each step to one row per user (min timestamp) before joining, or count DISTINCT user_id.

gotchas.trap: Showing last week's 7-day funnel conversion as final.
gotchas.correct: Only report cohorts whose full window has elapsed, or mark the period as incomplete.

Write the naive "count per event" funnel and the anchored 7-day funnel from this lesson, and explain every difference in the counts. Then change the window to 14 days and confirm only the late converters move.

lessons.title: Cohort retention: tables, curves, bounded and unbounded
lessons.summary: Build a cohort retention table in SQL, read it as curves, choose between N-day (bounded) and unbounded retention, and avoid the right-censoring trap.

sections.heading: Cohorts, buckets and the return event
A weekly retention table in Postgres
sections.body:
~~~sql
WITH births AS (
  SELECT user_id, date_trunc('week', min(ts)) AS cohort_week
  FROM events WHERE event = 'signup_completed'
  GROUP BY user_id
), active AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT user_id, date_trunc('week', ts) AS active_week
  FROM events WHERE event = 'document_edited'
)
SELECT b.cohort_week::date AS cohort,
       (a.active_week::date - b.cohort_week::date) / 7 AS week_n,
       count(DISTINCT a.user_id) AS retained
FROM births b
JOIN active a ON a.user_id = b.user_id AND a.active_week >= b.cohort_week
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2;
~~~

Divide `retained` by the cohort size to get rates. `date_trunc('week', ...)` truncates to the Monday of the ISO week, and on a `timestamptz` it truncates in the session time zone, so fix the time zone your team reports in.

sections.heading: N-day versus unbounded retention
sections.body:
- **N-day (bounded)** retention for week N: the share of the cohort active **in exactly week N**. Mixpanel calls this the **"On"** setting.
- **Unbounded** retention for week N: the share active **in week N or any later week**. Mixpanel's default **"On or After"** works this way, and Amplitude also offers N-day, unbounded and custom bracket retention.

Unbounded retention is never lower than N-day for the same bucket and can only stay flat or fall as N grows, because "active at N or later" includes "active at N+1 or later". It answers "have they left for good?" and is kind to infrequent-use products. N-day answers "are they using it in that period?" and fits habitual products. Pick one per metric, write it down, and never compare a bounded curve with an unbounded one.

~~~sql
-- Unbounded: user counts for week n if their last active week is >= n
WITH last_seen AS (
  SELECT b.user_id, b.cohort_week,
         (max(a.active_week)::date - b.cohort_week::date) / 7 AS last_week_n
  FROM births b JOIN active a USING (user_id)
  GROUP BY b.user_id, b.cohort_week
)
SELECT cohort_week::date, n,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE last_week_n >= n) AS retained_unbounded
FROM last_seen CROSS JOIN generate_series(0, 8) AS n
GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY 1, 2;
~~~

sections.heading: Rolling versus calendar buckets
sections.body: "Day 1" can mean two things. In Mixpanel's **rolling** mode Day 1 is **24 to 48 hours after birth**, and Week 1 is days 7 to 14. In **calendar** mode buckets follow calendar days instead, so a user who signs up at 23:00 and returns at 09:00 is "Day 1" in calendar mode but still "Day 0" in rolling mode. The `date_trunc` query above is calendar-based. State which one you use.

sections.heading: Reading the table without fooling yourself
sections.body:
The table is a triangle: the newest cohort has only week 0, the oldest has many weeks. Cells a cohort has **not reached yet** are unknown, not zero. If you average a column across cohorts, include only cohorts old enough to have that column, or the curve bends down artificially (right-censoring). Mixpanel's average retention works this way: it counts only completed time periods and marks incomplete buckets with an asterisk.

Read the table two ways. **Down a column**: is week-4 retention better for newer cohorts? That tells you whether product changes help. **Along a row**: does the curve flatten into a plateau? A curve that levels off shows a retained core. One that keeps sliding toward zero shows the product is not yet retaining anyone durably. Always show cohort sizes next to rates.

keyPoints: Define birth event, return event, bucket size and bounded vs unbounded before computing retention.
N-day (Mixpanel "On") counts activity in exactly bucket N; unbounded (Mixpanel default "On or After") counts bucket N or later.
Unbounded retention is always at least N-day retention for the same bucket and never rises with N.
Mixpanel rolling Day 1 is 24-48 hours after birth; calendar mode uses calendar days.
Cells a cohort has not reached are missing, not zero: exclude them from averages.

gotchas.trap: Averaging the week-8 column over all cohorts, including ones only 3 weeks old.
gotchas.correct: Average only cohorts that are at least 8 weeks old; leave unreached cells blank.

gotchas.trap: Comparing your SQL N-day curve with a tool report left on its default unbounded setting.
gotchas.correct: Match the definition: Mixpanel "On" for N-day, "On or After" for unbounded.

gotchas.trap: Using "any event" as the return event, so a push-notification open counts as retention.
gotchas.correct: Pick a return event that reflects real value and write it into the metric definition.

Then compute a naive column average that includes unreached cells as 0 and compare it with the censoring-aware average.

lessons.title: Window functions for sessions, streaks and time between events
lessons.summary: Use LAG, LEAD, ROW_NUMBER and running sums to build sessions, find streaks with gaps-and-islands, and measure time between events, while avoiding frame and partition traps.

sections.heading: How window functions work
sections.body:
A window function computes a value for each row from a set of related rows, without collapsing them like `GROUP BY` does. `PARTITION BY` says which rows belong together (usually one user), and `ORDER BY` inside `OVER` gives them an order.

Window functions run **after** `WHERE`, `GROUP BY` and `HAVING`. You cannot filter on them in the same query's `WHERE`. Compute them in a CTE or subquery and filter outside:

~~~sql
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT *, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts, event_id) AS rn
  FROM events
)
SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1;   -- first event per user
~~~

Add a unique tie-breaker (such as `event_id`) to the `ORDER BY` so the result is deterministic when two events share a timestamp.

sections.heading: Time between events with LAG and LEAD
sections.body:
`lag(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts)` returns the previous event's time for the same user. `ts - lag(ts)` is the gap. The first row of each partition gets NULL, which is correct: there is no previous event.

Forgetting `PARTITION BY user_id` is the classic bug. The "previous row" is then whichever user's event happened just before, and you measure gaps between strangers.

~~~sql
SELECT user_id, ts,
       ts - lag(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts) AS gap
FROM events;
~~~

sections.heading: Sessionization: flag and running sum
sections.body:
A common session rule: a new session starts when the gap since the user's previous event exceeds 30 minutes. Do it in two steps: flag session starts, then turn the flags into a session number with a running sum.

~~~sql
WITH flagged AS (
  SELECT user_id, ts, event_id,
         CASE WHEN ts - lag(ts) OVER w <= interval '30 minutes'
              THEN 0 ELSE 1 END AS is_new
  FROM events
  WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts, event_id)
)
SELECT user_id, ts,
       sum(is_new) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts, event_id
                         ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS session_n
FROM flagged;
~~~

The first event's `lag` is NULL, the comparison is NULL, so `CASE` falls to `ELSE 1`: every user's first event starts session 1. Session length is then `max(ts) - min(ts)` grouped by `(user_id, session_n)`.

sections.heading: Frames: the default you need to know
sections.body:
For aggregates and functions like `last_value`, the **frame** decides which rows are used. In PostgreSQL, if `ORDER BY` is given, the default frame runs from the start of the partition **through the current row plus its peers** (rows with an equal sort key). Without `ORDER BY` the frame is the whole partition.

Two consequences:

- `last_value(x) OVER (PARTITION BY u ORDER BY ts)` returns the *current* row's value (or its last peer), not the partition's last value. Add `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING`, or use `first_value` with descending order.
- A running sum with tied timestamps gives tied rows the same total, because peers are in each other's frame. Use a `ROWS` frame and a tie-breaker when you need a strict row-by-row count.

sections.heading: Streaks with gaps-and-islands
sections.body:
To find consecutive active days, first reduce to **one row per user per day**, then subtract a row number from the date. Consecutive days share the same result, which identifies the island.

~~~sql
WITH days AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT user_id, (ts AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date AS d FROM events
), grp AS (
  SELECT user_id, d,
         d - (row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY d))::int AS island
  FROM days
)
SELECT user_id, min(d) AS streak_start, max(d) AS streak_end, count(*) AS days
FROM grp GROUP BY user_id, island
ORDER BY days DESC;
~~~

Skipping the `DISTINCT` step breaks it: two events on the same day get different row numbers, so the same date lands in two islands.

keyPoints: Window functions keep rows; PARTITION BY groups them and ORDER BY in OVER orders them.
Window functions run after WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING, so filter on them in an outer query.
LAG/LEAD give previous/next values; always partition by user when measuring gaps.
Sessions: flag gaps above a threshold, then a running sum of flags gives a session number.
Default frame with ORDER BY ends at the current row and its peers; widen it for last_value.
Streaks: one row per user-day, then date minus row_number identifies consecutive runs.

gotchas.trap: Writing WHERE row_number() OVER (...) = 1.
gotchas.correct: Compute row_number in a CTE or subquery and filter rn = 1 in the outer query.

gotchas.trap: Using last_value with only ORDER BY and expecting the last row of the partition.
gotchas.correct: Specify ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING, or use first_value with reversed order.

gotchas.trap: Running gaps-and-islands directly on raw events.
gotchas.correct: Deduplicate to one row per user per day before subtracting row_number.

gotchas.trap: Omitting PARTITION BY user_id in lag().
gotchas.correct: Partition by the entity whose gaps you measure, or you compare different users' events.

Build sessions with a 30-minute rule, report median session length and sessions per user, then compute each user's longest daily streak with gaps-and-islands. Finally introduce duplicate timestamps and show how the default RANGE frame changes a running count compared with a ROWS frame and tie-breaker.

lessons.title: Segmentation traps: Simpson's paradox, survivorship and selection
lessons.summary: Why breaking a metric down by segment can reverse its story, and how survivorship, self-selection and post-treatment segments mislead product decisions.

sections.heading: Why segment at all
sections.body: An overall metric hides who is moving. Segmenting by platform, plan, country or acquisition channel shows where a change helps and where it hurts. But every segmentation is a new analysis with its own traps, and the more slices you look at, the more likely one looks remarkable by chance. Decide the important segments in advance and report segment sizes next to rates. Microsoft's ExP paper on metric interpretation pitfalls lists Simpson's paradox among the twelve common ways metrics mislead.

sections.heading: Simpson's paradox
sections.body:
A trend that holds in every segment can reverse in the total when the **mix** of segments differs between the groups being compared.

| Segment | Flow A | Flow B |
|---|---|---|
| Desktop | 400 / 1,000 = 40% | 90 / 200 = 45% |
| Mobile | 20 / 200 = 10% | 120 / 1,000 = 12% |
| **Total** | **420 / 1,200 = 35%** | **210 / 1,200 = 17.5%** |

Flow B wins on desktop and on mobile, yet loses overall, because most of B's traffic was mobile, which converts worse everywhere. The fix is not to pick the "right" number by taste. Ask why the mix differs (a ramp to one platform? an experiment bug?), compare within segments, and if you need one number, weight segments by a common mix. In a randomized experiment, a large mix difference is itself a warning sign that assignment or logging is broken.

sections.heading: Survivorship bias
sections.body: Survivorship bias is analysing only the units that made it through some filter. "Our current customers rate pricing 4.6/5" ignores everyone who churned over pricing. "Long-tenured users all use feature X" says nothing about whether X kept them, because users who left are not in the table. Watch for filters like `WHERE status = 'active'`, "users with at least one session this month", or survey data that only current users can answer. Start from the full cohort at the beginning of the period and follow it forward.

sections.heading: Selection bias and self-selection
sections.body:
Users choose which features to adopt. People who connect an integration or invite teammates are already more engaged, so "adopters retain twice as well" mixes the feature's effect with who chooses it. The comparison groups were not formed at random.

Safer approaches, from strongest to weakest: run a randomized experiment (d4); compare adopters with similar non-adopters on **pre-adoption** behaviour; or at least look at whether adopters were already retaining better before they adopted. Present observational segment differences as hypotheses, not effects.

sections.heading: Do not segment on something the change affects
sections.body: Segments must be defined by attributes fixed **before** the change or exposure: signup platform, country, plan at start, acquisition channel. Segmenting on something the change itself can move (such as "users who reached 3 sessions in week 1" after a launch that changes how many reach 3 sessions) changes **who is in the segment**, and the comparison is no longer like for like.

keyPoints: Choose key segments up front; slicing many ways invites chance findings.
Simpson's paradox: segment-level effects can reverse in aggregate when segment mix differs.
Survivorship bias: filtering to current or active users drops those who left for the reason you study.
Self-selected adopters differ from non-adopters before adoption; observational gaps are not causal effects.
Define segments using attributes fixed before the change, never ones the change can affect.

gotchas.trap: Declaring flow B worse because its overall rate is lower, when it wins in every segment.
gotchas.correct: Check the segment mix, compare within segments, and investigate why the mix differs.

gotchas.trap: Measuring satisfaction with a pricing change by surveying current customers only.
gotchas.correct: Include churned customers (e.g. exit surveys, churn rate by cohort) or the result is survivorship-biased.

gotchas.trap: Claiming a feature causes retention because its adopters retain better.
gotchas.correct: Treat it as a hypothesis; test with an experiment or compare on pre-adoption behaviour.

lessons.lab: Recreate the Simpson's paradox table in SQL from row-level synthetic data, then compute a mix-weighted conversion for each flow using a fixed 50/50 desktop/mobile mix. Next, build a synthetic dataset where engaged users are more likely to adopt a feature that has no effect, and show the "adopters retain better" gap appearing anyway.

lessons.title: Dashboards that answer questions
lessons.summary: Design dashboards around decisions: one question per chart, annotations for releases and tracking changes, honest axes, visible denominators and incomplete periods, and accessible text alternatives.

sections.heading: Start from the decision
sections.body:
A dashboard that "shows everything" is checked once and then ignored. Start instead from the decisions it supports: "Do we keep investing in onboarding?", "Is the new pricing hurting conversion?". For each decision, one chart answers one question, with a clear metric definition, an owner and, where it helps, the threshold that would trigger action. Microsoft ExP's STEDII list includes **interpretability and actionability**: a metric people cannot act on is noise on the page.

A practical test: for each chart, write down what you would do if the line went up, and what you would do if it went down. If both answers are "nothing", remove the chart.

sections.heading: Annotate what changed
sections.body: Most surprising steps in a chart are not user behaviour. They are a release, a marketing push, an outage, or a **tracking change** (a renamed event, a new SDK, consent banner changes, bot filtering). Put annotations on the time axis for releases and instrumentation changes, so nobody spends a week explaining a jump that a schema change caused. Check data-quality signals before reading the business metric, as the ExP pitfalls paper recommends for experiments.

sections.heading: Honest axes and honest periods
sections.body:
- **Bar charts start at zero.** Bar length encodes the value. Starting the axis at 40% makes 42% versus 45% look like a doubling.
- **Line charts** can use a narrower range to show change, but label the axis clearly and avoid switching ranges between charts that people compare.
- **Avoid dual y-axes** for unrelated metrics. The visual crossing point is arbitrary and depends on how each axis was scaled.
- **Mark incomplete periods.** The current week or month is partial, so its totals look like a drop. Exclude it, show it dashed, or label it "to date". The same applies to recent retention cells and funnel windows that are still open.
- **Show the denominator.** A rate without its count hides whether a change is two users or two thousand.

sections.heading: Accessible charts
sections.body: A chart is a complex image. W3C WAI's guidance is to give complex images a short text alternative plus a longer description that conveys the same information, for example the underlying data table or a summary of the trend. In practice: a title that states the question, a one-line takeaway, a data table or download, and colour choices that do not rely on colour alone to separate series.

keyPoints: Each chart answers one question tied to a decision, with a defined metric and an owner.
Annotate releases, campaigns, outages and tracking changes on the time axis.
Bars start at zero; label line-chart ranges; avoid dual axes for unrelated metrics.
Mark or exclude incomplete periods so partial data does not look like a drop.
Show denominators and provide a text description or data table for charts.

gotchas.trap: Adding every available metric so the dashboard is "complete".
gotchas.correct: Keep only charts whose movement would change a decision.

gotchas.trap: Reading a sudden jump in signups as a growth win without checking instrumentation.
gotchas.correct: Check and annotate tracking and release changes first.

gotchas.trap: Plotting the current, partial week next to full weeks.
gotchas.correct: Exclude it, draw it differently, or label it as to-date.

lessons.lab: Take one of the queries from this domain (funnel or retention) and design a single dashboard tile for it: write the decision it supports, the exact metric definition, the axis choices, an annotation list for the last quarter, how the partial period is shown, and a two-sentence text alternative. Have a teammate read only the tile and state the decision it implies.

lessons.title: Designing an A/B test that can answer a question
lessons.summary: Write a falsifiable hypothesis, pick the unit of randomisation, separate the primary metric from guardrail and data-quality metrics, and fix the minimum detectable effect before launch.

sections.heading: Start from a falsifiable hypothesis
sections.body:
An experiment is only as good as the decision it is built to make. Write the hypothesis before you build the variant:

> Because **[evidence]**, changing **[thing]** for **[population]** will move **[primary metric]** by at least **[MDE]**, without degrading **[guardrails]**.

This one sentence fixes the population, the metric you will judge on, the smallest effect worth shipping, and the things that must not break. "Ship the new onboarding and see what moves" fixes none of them. It invites you to scan dozens of metrics afterwards and keep whichever one happens to look good.

sections.heading: Choose the unit of randomisation
sections.body:
The **unit of randomisation** is the thing you assign to control or treatment: a user, a device, a session, or a group such as a workspace or tenant.

- **User (stable ID)** is the default for product changes. Each person sees one consistent experience.
- **Session or page view** gives more units, but the same person can see both variants. Only use it for changes a user will not notice across visits.
- **Group (workspace, tenant, account)** is needed when users in the same group affect each other, for example in a shared document or a team setting. Randomising individuals would let teammates see different versions, and the variants would contaminate each other.

PostHog feature flags hash the flag key with the distinct ID to assign a bucket. For a shared feature, evaluate the flag at the group level instead, so a whole account gets the same variant. Microsoft Research points out that tenant-randomised tests have far fewer units than user-level tests, so they need more care with power.

sections.heading: Three kinds of metric
sections.body:
Microsoft ExP sorts experiment metrics into three groups:

| Kind | Purpose | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Data-quality | Can the result be trusted at all? | Sample ratio mismatch (SRM), data loss, join rates |
| OEC / primary | The goal the decision is based on | Checkout conversion, weekly active teams |
| Guardrail | Must not get worse | Page load time, crash rate, abandonment |

Check data-quality metrics **first**. If the split is wrong, nothing else on the scorecard means anything. Then read the one primary metric you named in advance. Guardrails are not things to maximise. They are tripwires: if one degrades significantly, the change does not ship as is, even when the primary metric improves.

sections.heading: Fix the minimum detectable effect
sections.body:
The **minimum detectable effect (MDE)** is the smallest true effect the test is designed to detect with the chosen power, usually 80%, at the chosen significance level, usually 5%. Pick it from the business case: "a lift smaller than 1 percentage point would not pay for the extra maintenance".

The MDE drives sample size, and the relationship is steep. Required sample size scales with **1 / MDE²**, so halving the MDE roughly quadruples the users you need. PostHog's planner uses a default MDE of 30% relative when you have not set one.

keyPoints: The hypothesis names the population, the primary metric, the MDE and the guardrails before launch.
Randomise at the level where users influence each other: user by default, workspace or tenant for shared features.
Read data-quality metrics (SRM first), then the primary metric, then guardrails.
Guardrails are tripwires, not goals.
Sample size scales with 1/MDE²: halve the MDE and you need about 4x the traffic.

gotchas.trap: Choose the primary metric after seeing which one moved most.
gotchas.correct: Name one primary metric before launch. Metrics picked afterwards are exploratory only.

gotchas.trap: Randomise individual users for a collaborative feature to get more units.
gotchas.correct: Randomise by workspace or tenant when users in a group affect each other, and plan for the lower unit count.

gotchas.trap: Treat a guardrail like a secondary goal that can be traded away.
gotchas.correct: A significant guardrail regression blocks shipping the variant as is.

lessons.lab: Write a one-page test plan for a change in your own product: hypothesis sentence, unit of randomisation with a reason, one primary metric, two guardrails, the data-quality checks you will run first, and an MDE justified by cost. Ask a teammate to find anything they could change after the test starts. Anything they find goes into the plan.
