lessons.title: Sample size, power and the small-product problem
lessons.summary: Compute sample size from baseline rate, MDE, alpha and power, see why small products cannot detect small lifts, and learn what to do instead.

sections.heading: The formula
sections.body:
For a conversion metric with baseline rate p1 and target rate p2, the per-arm sample size for a two-sided test is:

```text
n = (z_{1-α/2} + z_{power})² × [p1(1-p1) + p2(1-p2)] / (p2 - p1)²
```

With α = 0.05 and 80% power, z = 1.960 and 0.842, so (1.960 + 0.842)² ≈ 7.85.

Worked example: p1 = 10%, p2 = 12% (a 20% relative lift).

- Variance sum = 0.09 + 0.1056 = 0.1956
- n = 7.85 × 0.1956 / 0.0004 ≈ **3,839 per arm**

sections.heading: The rule of thumb
sections.body:
PostHog's planner uses **N = 16 × variance / d²** per variant, for 80% power and 95% confidence, with variance p(1-p) for funnel metrics. For the same example, 16 × 0.09 / 0.0004 = **3,600 per variant**, which is the example in PostHog's docs.

The "16" is 2 × 7.85 ≈ 15.7, rounded up. The rule uses only the baseline variance, so when the treatment rate is higher than baseline it slightly **undercounts**, as here: 3,600 vs 3,839. Use the rule for a quick estimate and the exact formula when the number matters.

sections.heading: Why small products struggle
sections.body:
Turn the formula around to ask what a fixed audience can detect. With **1,000 users per arm** and a 5% baseline, the smallest detectable absolute lift at α = 0.05 and 80% power is about **2.7 percentage points**. That is a **55% relative lift**. Most good product changes move conversion by a few percent, so a product of this size would almost never see a significant result from them.

Running the test anyway is not harmless. An underpowered test usually returns "not significant". When it does return a significant result, the estimated effect tends to be exaggerated, because only large noisy estimates clear the bar.

sections.heading: What to do instead
sections.body:
- **Test bolder changes.** A redesign of the pricing page can plausibly move conversion by 30%. A button colour cannot.
- **Use a more sensitive metric.** A metric close to the change, such as completion of the step you changed, has more signal than revenue at the end of the funnel. This assumes it is a valid leading indicator of the goal.
- **Reduce variance.** CUPED uses each user's pre-experiment behaviour as a covariate. Microsoft reported about a 50% variance reduction on Bing, which is like doubling traffic. PostHog and Amplitude both offer CUPED as an option.
- **Run longer**, if novelty and seasonality allow it.
- **Do not A/B test at all.** Use qualitative research, usability tests, and a staged rollout behind a flag with guardrail monitoring. Be honest that this is not causal proof.

Changing α after looking at the data, or splitting scarce traffic across more variants, makes the problem worse.

keyPoints: PostHog rule of thumb: 16 × p(1-p) / d² per variant. For 10% → 12% that is 3,600, and the exact formula gives 3,839.
With 1,000 users per arm at a 5% baseline, the MDE is about 2.7 pp (55% relative).
Underpowered tests miss real effects and exaggerate the ones they find.
Options for small products: bolder changes, sensitive metrics, CUPED, longer runs, or no A/B test.

gotchas.trap: Add more variants to "learn more" from a small audience.
gotchas.correct: Every extra arm cuts the per-arm sample and lowers power. Use fewer arms when traffic is scarce.

gotchas.trap: A non-significant result from an underpowered test means the change does nothing.
gotchas.correct: It means the test could not tell. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.

gotchas.trap: The 16σ²/d² rule is exact.
gotchas.correct: It is an approximation that uses only baseline variance and can undercount slightly when the treatment rate is higher.

lessons.lab: In Python with scipy (the runner has 1.13), write `n_per_arm(p1, p2, alpha=0.05, power=0.8)` using `scipy.stats.norm.ppf`. Check that it returns about 3,839 for 0.10 → 0.12 and compare it with 16·p(1-p)/d². Then write the inverse, `mde(n, p1)`, and confirm that n = 1,000 at p1 = 0.05 gives about 0.0273. Plot MDE against n for your own baseline rate and mark your weekly traffic on the chart.

lessons.title: Reading results: significance, intervals, peeking and many metrics
lessons.summary: Interpret p-values and confidence intervals correctly, see how peeking inflates false positives, use sequential tests when you need to look early, and control error across many metrics.

sections.heading: p-values and confidence intervals
sections.body:
Example: control converts 400/4,000 (10.0%) and treatment 460/4,000 (11.5%). A two-proportion z-test gives **z = 2.17, p = 0.030**. The 95% confidence interval for the difference is **[0.14 pp, 2.86 pp]**.

What this says:

- If there were no true difference, a result at least this extreme would happen about 3% of the time.
- The data are consistent with true lifts anywhere from about 0.1 pp to about 2.9 pp.

What it does **not** say: that there is a 97% chance B is better, or that the lift is 15%. The point estimate is a 15% relative lift, but the lower end of the interval is tiny. If the change costs something to keep, compare the **interval** with your MDE, not just the p-value with 0.05.

In scipy, `chi2_contingency(table, correction=False)` gives the same p-value as the hand z-test.

sections.heading: Peeking
sections.body: A fixed-horizon test is valid only if you analyse it once, at the planned sample size. If you check repeatedly and stop the first time p < 0.05, the false-positive rate rises fast. In this course's simulation of an A/A test (no true effect) with **10 equally spaced looks**, stopping at the first |z| > 1.96 gave a false-positive rate of **19.7%**, compared with 4.8% when looking only at the end.

sections.heading: Sequential testing
sections.body:
If you need to look early, for example to stop a harmful change fast, use a method built for it. The mixture sequential probability ratio test (**mSPRT**, Johari et al.) gives **always-valid** p-values and intervals, so you can check at any time without inflating error.

**Amplitude Experiment uses sequential testing (mSPRT) by default.** A Welch's T-test is an option. Amplitude's duration estimator only supports the T-test. **PostHog** offers a **Bayesian engine (the default)** and a frequentist one. The Bayesian engine reports a chance to win and a credible interval. Know which one your tool runs before you read its dashboard.

sections.heading: Many metrics, many variants
sections.body:
With k independent metrics each tested at α = 0.05, the chance that at least one is a false positive is 1 - 0.95^k: **40% for 10 metrics and 64% for 20**. A scorecard of 20 metrics where one is green is weak evidence.

- **Pre-register one primary metric.** Treat the rest as guardrails or exploratory.
- **Bonferroni** (test each at α/k) controls the family-wise error rate but is conservative. Amplitude lets you turn it on.
- **Benjamini-Hochberg** controls the false discovery rate and is less strict (`scipy.stats.false_discovery_control`). For p = [0.001, 0.008, 0.039, 0.041, 0.042, 0.06, ...], BH at q = 0.05 keeps only the first **two**. Five of them were below 0.05 before correction.

PostHog does **not** correct for multiple comparisons across variants or metrics, and it allows up to 19 test variants plus control. With many arms, you have to do the correction yourself.

keyPoints: p = 0.03 does not mean a 97% chance that B is better. Compare the CI with your MDE.
Peeking at 10 looks inflated A/A false positives from about 5% to about 20% in simulation.
mSPRT gives always-valid results and is Amplitude Experiment's default.
PostHog: Bayesian by default, frequentist optional, no multiple-comparison correction.
FWER = 1 - 0.95^k. Use one primary metric, and Bonferroni or BH for families.

gotchas.trap: Stop the test as soon as the dashboard turns significant.
gotchas.correct: With a fixed-horizon test, analyse once at the planned sample size, or use a sequential method designed for continuous monitoring.

gotchas.trap: p = 0.03 means a 3% chance the null is true.
gotchas.correct: It is the probability of data this extreme if the null were true. It is not the probability that the null is true.

gotchas.trap: Any green metric on a 20-metric scorecard is a win.
gotchas.correct: Expect about one false positive among 20 at α = 0.05. Judge on the pre-registered primary metric and correct the rest.

lessons.lab: Using numpy and scipy 1.13: (1) reproduce the 400/4000 vs 460/4000 z-test and CI by hand, then check the p-value against `chi2_contingency(correction=False)`; (2) simulate 20,000 A/A tests with 10 looks at 500 users per arm per look (`np.random.default_rng(42)`) and measure the false-positive rate with and without peeking; (3) run `false_discovery_control` on the 10 p-values in this lesson and list which ones survive at q = 0.05.

lessons.title: Pitfalls, feature flags and when not to A/B test
lessons.summary: Detect sample ratio mismatch, separate novelty and primacy from lasting effects, handle interference and bucketing bugs, and use staged rollouts when an A/B test is the wrong tool.

sections.heading: Sample ratio mismatch
sections.body:
If you planned a 50/50 split and see **50,500 vs 49,500**, a chi-square goodness-of-fit test gives χ² = 10.0, **p ≈ 0.0016**. A 1% imbalance on 100,000 users is very unlikely to be chance. That is an **SRM**. Stop reading the results and debug, because whatever caused the imbalance can also bias the metrics.

Microsoft ExP's SRM taxonomy groups the causes by stage:

- **Assignment:** a bucketing bug, or the variants started at different times.
- **Execution:** a treatment redirect or crash that loses users before the exposure event fires.
- **Log processing:** bot filtering or deduplication that treats the arms differently.
- **Analysis:** a trigger condition that depends on the treatment.

Always compare the planned split with the actual one before anything else. Do not "reweight" an SRM away: the users who went missing are not a random sample.

sections.heading: Novelty, primacy and the long term
sections.body:
- **Novelty effect:** users click a new thing because it is new, and the lift fades.
- **Primacy (change aversion):** experienced users do worse at first because they are used to the old design, and they recover later.

Both mean the first week can mislead. Plot the treatment effect by day, and split it by new versus existing users. New users have no old habit to unlearn. Google's long-term ads study found that user learning "takes a long time to converge", so short tests can misjudge the long-term effect. For decisions with lasting effects, keep a **long-term holdout**: a small group that stays on control after you ship.

sections.heading: Interference
sections.body: A/B analysis assumes one unit's outcome does not depend on another unit's assignment. That breaks in marketplaces, social and collaborative products, and shared-inventory systems. Randomising by cluster (workspace or tenant) contains the spillover, but it gives you fewer, larger units and therefore less power. Microsoft Research describes why tenant-level tests are hard and why simple tenant pairing may not fix it.

sections.heading: Bucketing bugs and flags
sections.body:
PostHog assigns a flag value by hashing `"{flag_key}.{distinct_id}"` to a number in [0, 1]. Consequences:

- **Raising a rollout from 10% to 50% keeps the original 10% included.** Earlier users do not get reshuffled.
- **Identity changes can move users.** When an anonymous visitor signs up and becomes identified, the distinct ID changes, and the user can land in a different variant. When the experiment spans that moment, use device bucketing (which hashes the stable `$device_id`), or call `identify()` before any flag is evaluated. PostHog cautions against relying on experience continuity (flag persistence across authentication) because values can still change after `identify()`.
- **Reusing a flag key** for a new experiment reuses the same buckets, so earlier experiences carry over.

sections.heading: When not to A/B test

keyPoints: Test the split first. 50,500 vs 49,500 gives p ≈ 0.0016: an SRM, so stop and debug.
SRM causes: assignment, execution, log processing, analysis.
Look for novelty and primacy by plotting the effect over time and splitting new vs existing users.
Cluster randomisation handles interference at a cost in power.
Hash-based flags keep earlier users when you raise a rollout. Identity changes can move users unless you use device bucketing or identify users before flags are evaluated.
Use staged rollouts for must-ship or low-traffic changes, and do not call them experiments.

gotchas.trap: A 1% split imbalance on 100k users is negligible.
gotchas.correct: It is highly significant (p ≈ 0.0016) and signals a bug that can bias every metric.

gotchas.trap: Kill a redesign that loses in week one.
gotchas.correct: Check for primacy: look at the trend over time and at new users before deciding.

gotchas.trap: A gradual rollout with before/after numbers is an A/B test.
gotchas.correct: Without a concurrent randomised control it is not causal evidence.

Show that raising the threshold from 0.1 to 0.5 keeps every user who was already included. Then show that switching from an anonymous ID to a user ID moves about half of the people who change ID to the other arm of a 50/50 flag.

lessons.title: Growth loops, referrals and an honest K-factor
lessons.summary: How loops differ from funnels, the four common loop types, and how to measure referral and network effects without fooling yourself.

sections.heading: Funnels describe, loops compound
sections.body:
A **funnel** is a one-way path: visitors come in at the top, some drop out at each step, and what comes out the bottom is the result. A funnel says nothing about where the *next* visitors come from.

A **growth loop** is a closed cycle in which the output of one cohort becomes the input of the next. A new user does something (publishes, invites, pays) that brings in more new users, who do the same thing.

The practical difference is what you optimise. In a funnel you push conversion at each step. In a loop you also care about:

- **Loop yield**: how many new inputs one cycle produces per user.
- **Cycle time**: how long one turn of the loop takes. Two loops with the same yield compound at very different speeds if one turns weekly and the other quarterly.
- **Leakage**: where in the cycle users stop before they feed the next turn.

"Growth loops" and "AARRR" are industry frameworks rather than standards, so this course defines them in its own words. Funnels are still how you *measure* each step inside a loop.

sections.heading: Four common loop types
sections.body:
| Loop | One turn | Typical input metric |
|---|---|---|
| **Viral / referral** | A user invites or shares, and an invitee signs up and activates | Invites sent per activated user, invite-to-activation rate |
| **Content (user- or company-generated)** | Someone creates a public page, search or social brings visitors, and some sign up and create more | Indexable pages created, visits per page, visit-to-signup rate |
| **Paid** | Revenue from customers funds ads, and ads bring customers whose margin funds more ads | CAC by channel, payback period |
| **Sales-led** | Product usage or marketing produces qualified accounts, sales closes them, and revenue funds more reps or marketing | Qualified accounts per period, win rate, sales cycle length |

Most products have one dominant loop and a few weaker ones. Choose loop input metrics the way Amplitude suggests choosing North Star inputs: a small set (it suggests 3 to 5) that the team can move, covering breadth, depth, frequency and efficiency.

sections.heading: K-factor and what it does and does not tell you
sections.body:
The usual definition, used here as a course convention, is:

**K = invites sent per user × conversion rate of an invite into a new (activated) user**

If 100 activated users each send 3 invites and 10% of invites turn into activated users, K = 3 × 0.10 = **0.3**.

- **K < 1 still helps.** If K stays steady, every seed user brings 1/(1 − K) users in total. At K = 0.3 that is about 1.43, so 100 paid signups become about 143 users.
- **K ≥ 1** means self-sustaining growth. It rarely lasts, because the pool of reachable people runs out and K falls over time.
- K ignores **cycle time**. A K of 0.5 that turns in a day beats a K of 0.7 that turns in six months over most planning horizons.

sections.heading: Measuring K honestly
sections.body:
Reported K-factors are often inflated. Check these before you trust one:

1. **Count activated invitees, not signups.** Use a funnel from invite sent to invitee activated with an explicit conversion window. A window that is too short hides slow converters. A window that is unlimited lets unrelated signups creep in.
2. **Exclude self-referrals and duplicate accounts** made to claim a reward.
3. **Measure incrementality.** Some "referred" users would have signed up anyway, for example a colleague who was already evaluating the product. A holdout, where some users never see the referral prompt, estimates the lift the programme actually causes.
4. **Report by cohort and over time.** Early adopters invite more than later users, so a single blended K overstates the future.
5. **Watch for interference in experiments.** Invitees in the control group can be exposed to treatment users' invites, so user-level randomisation leaks. Microsoft's ExP team describes why tenant- or cluster-level randomisation is harder and what goes wrong with it.

sections.heading: Network effects
sections.body:
A **network effect** means each new user makes the product more valuable to existing users (shared workspaces, marketplaces, integrations). It is different from virality: virality is about *acquisition*, network effects are about *value and retention*.

Measure network effects through retention and engagement as density grows. One example is retention of accounts by number of active teammates. Remember that this is correlational: bigger teams may retain better for other reasons, such as company size.

keyPoints: A funnel is one-way; a loop feeds its output back as the next input.
Judge loops by yield and cycle time, not just step conversion.
K = invites per user × invite-to-activated-user conversion (course convention).
With a steady K below 1, each seed user brings 1/(1 − K) users in total.
Honest K counts activated invitees in a set window, removes self-referrals, and checks incrementality with a holdout.
Referral experiments can leak across users; consider cluster-level randomisation.

gotchas.trap: K below 1 means referrals are worthless.
gotchas.correct: A steady K below 1 still multiplies every acquired user by 1/(1 − K), which lowers effective CAC.

gotchas.trap: Counting every signup with a referral code as a viral conversion.
gotchas.correct: Count activated invitees within a set window, remove self-referrals, and estimate incrementality with a holdout.

gotchas.trap: Comparing loops on K alone.
gotchas.correct: Cycle time matters as much: a faster loop with lower K can compound faster.

Then recompute it after removing invitees whose email domain and device match the inviter, and compare the two.

lessons.title: Onboarding, time-to-value and activation experiments
lessons.summary: Define activation, shorten time-to-value, and run activation experiments that still mean something on a small product.

sections.heading: Activation and time-to-value
sections.body:
**Activation** is the first moment a new user gets the core value of the product, defined as a specific event (for example "first deploy succeeded" or "first report shared"). **Time-to-value (TTV)** is the time from signup to that event.

To choose an activation event:

1. List candidate early actions.
2. Compare later retention for users who did versus did not do each action in their first days.
3. Pick an action that is strongly associated with retention *and* that the product can make easier.

That association is correlational. Users who were already motivated do more of everything. Confirm with an experiment that making the action easier also improves retention.

sections.heading: Measuring onboarding with funnels
sections.body:
Model onboarding as an ordered funnel (signup, connect data, first success) and read both conversion and **time to convert**.

The conversion window matters. Mixpanel funnels default to a **7-day** window. If many developers finish setup on day 9 or 10, a 7-day funnel undercounts activation, and a change that only speeds people up can look like a conversion win. Set the window to match how long real setup takes, and keep it fixed when you compare periods.

Read retention with a stated definition as well. In Mixpanel, "On or After" (unbounded) and "On" (exactly that bucket) give different numbers for the same users.

sections.heading: Shortening time-to-value
sections.body:
Common levers, roughly in order of how often they work:

- **Remove steps** before first value: defer profile setup, billing and invitations until after the first success.
- **Templates, sample data or a sandbox**, so users see value before they connect their own systems.
- **Opinionated defaults** instead of empty configuration screens.
- **Contextual help** at the step where the funnel drops, rather than a long upfront tour.

Be careful with "forced" activation. Making an action mandatory (for example a required invite step) raises the activation metric by definition, but it can break the link to retention that made the metric useful. That is Goodhart's law: once a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure.

sections.heading: Activation experiments on small products
sections.body:
Activation experiments usually randomise new signups, so traffic is limited. PostHog's rule of thumb is N ≈ 16·p(1 − p)/d² per variant (80% power, 95% confidence). Computed for this course: with 1,000 users per arm and a 5% baseline, the smallest detectable lift is about **2.7 percentage points, roughly 55% relative**.

What to do about it:

- Test **bold** changes that could plausibly move the metric a lot, not button copy.
- Use a **more sensitive** primary metric earlier in the funnel (for example setup-step completion), and keep retention as a guardrail you watch over a longer window.
- Fix the sample size in advance. Don't stop as soon as the result looks significant.
- Add qualitative evidence (session reviews, interviews) where tests cannot reach power.

Watch for **novelty effects**. A new onboarding flow can lift early numbers while users learn it, and Google's long-term study found user learning can take a long time to settle. Check retention cohorts after the launch, not just week one.

keyPoints: Activation is a specific event that marks first value; TTV is time from signup to it.
Pick activation events by their link to retention, then validate causally with an experiment.
Set funnel conversion windows to match real setup time; Mixpanel defaults to 7 days.
Forcing the activation action games the metric (Goodhart).
Small products should test big changes and use sensitive upstream metrics with retention guardrails.

gotchas.trap: The users who do X retain better, so making X mandatory will raise retention.
gotchas.correct: That link is correlational. Test it, and watch retention rather than only the activation metric.

gotchas.trap: Comparing onboarding funnels without checking the conversion window.
gotchas.correct: Use a window that fits real setup time, and keep it the same across comparisons.

gotchas.trap: Calling an onboarding redesign a win from its first week of data.
gotchas.correct: Novelty can inflate early results; follow retention cohorts after launch.

lessons.lab: Build a signup → connect_source → first_success funnel with 7-day and 21-day windows on the same cohort. Report how much activation the 7-day window misses, then use the PostHog rule of thumb to compute the per-arm sample size needed to detect a 20% relative lift at your baseline.

lessons.title: SEO and content for developer and B2B products
lessons.summary: Technical SEO basics, Core Web Vitals and rendering choices for docs, plus content that earns qualified developer traffic.

sections.heading: Why content matters for developer and B2B products
sections.body:
Developers and technical buyers often start in a search engine with a specific problem ("postgres connection pool exhausted", "webhook signature verification node"). Pages that solve that problem in your product's context can feed a **content loop**: useful pages bring visitors, some sign up, and their usage or questions point to the next pages.

Content that tends to work:

- **Documentation and guides** that answer real tasks, with runnable examples.
- **Integration pages** for each tool you connect to, written for someone evaluating that integration.
- **Comparison and migration guides** that are honest about trade-offs.
- **Public user-generated pages** (templates, public projects), but only where each page has unique value.

Avoid mass-produced thin or near-duplicate pages. They spread crawling and ranking signals thin and help nobody.

sections.heading: Technical SEO basics
sections.body:
- **Crawlable, rendered HTML.** Make sure the content exists in the HTML that a crawler gets. web.dev notes that crawlers can run JavaScript but often have limits on how they render, and that server-side rendering is a popular way to deliver complete-looking pages. For docs and marketing pages, prefer **static or server rendering**. Static rendering also gives a consistently fast TTFB.
- **One canonical URL per piece of content.** Duplicates (tracking parameters, trailing slashes, http/https) should consolidate. Google treats a redirect as a stronger signal than `rel="canonical"`, which is stronger than appearing in a sitemap. All of these are hints, not commands.
- **Sitemaps are hints too.** Google ignores `<priority>` and `<changefreq>` and uses `<lastmod>` only when it is accurate. One sitemap file holds at most 50,000 URLs or 50 MB uncompressed.
- **Keep pages out of the index with `noindex`**, not robots.txt. robots.txt controls crawling, and a blocked page can't show its noindex.

sections.heading: Core Web Vitals
sections.body:
Google's Core Web Vitals, with "good" thresholds from web.dev:

| Metric | Measures | Good |
|---|---|---|
| **LCP** (Largest Contentful Paint) | Loading | ≤ 2.5 s |
| **INP** (Interaction to Next Paint) | Responsiveness | ≤ 200 ms |
| **CLS** (Cumulative Layout Shift) | Visual stability | ≤ 0.1 |

Assess each one at the **75th percentile** of real page loads, separately for mobile and desktop. **INP replaced FID** as the responsiveness metric in 2024. A median from a single lab run on a fast laptop doesn't tell you whether real users get a good experience.

sections.heading: Measuring content as a channel
sections.body:
Track content the way you track any channel. Measure organic visits to each page group, then the visit-to-signup and signup-to-activation rates for visitors who landed there. Rankings and raw pageviews are vanity metrics if the visitors never activate.

Attribution is weak here, because content often gets the first touch and other channels get the last click. Use the incrementality ideas from the channel economics lesson before you cut or expand content spend.

keyPoints: Developer content works when it solves specific tasks: docs, integrations, honest comparisons.
Serve docs and marketing pages as static or server-rendered HTML.
Redirects beat rel=canonical, which beats sitemap inclusion; all are hints.
Sitemaps: priority and changefreq are ignored; lastmod only if accurate; 50,000 URLs or 50 MB per file.
Core Web Vitals good: LCP ≤ 2.5 s, INP ≤ 200 ms, CLS ≤ 0.1 at p75; INP replaced FID in 2024.

gotchas.trap: Using robots.txt to remove a page from search results.
gotchas.correct: Use noindex, and let the page be crawled so the noindex is seen.

gotchas.trap: Setting <priority>1.0</priority> on key pages to boost them.
gotchas.correct: Google ignores priority and changefreq; keep lastmod accurate instead.

gotchas.trap: Reporting median Lighthouse scores as Core Web Vitals.
gotchas.correct: Core Web Vitals are assessed on real-user data at the 75th percentile, split by device.

lessons.lab: Take one docs page and record its LCP, INP and CLS from field data at the 75th percentile for mobile. Then list every URL variant that serves the same content and decide, for each one, whether to redirect it or canonicalise it.

lessons.title: Channel economics: CAC by channel, attribution and incrementality
lessons.summary: Compute CAC and payback per channel, understand what attribution can and cannot tell you, and measure incremental lift.

sections.heading: CAC by channel, not blended
sections.body:
**CAC** = acquisition spend for a channel ÷ new customers that channel acquired, over the same period.

**Blended CAC** divides all spend by all new customers, including organic and word of mouth. It is fine for a board summary but bad for decisions, because organic customers make paid channels look cheaper than they are.

Example: $30,000 of paid spend brings 50 customers, and 100 more arrive organically.
- Blended CAC = 30,000 / 150 = **$200**.
- Paid CAC = 30,000 / 50 = **$600**.

Put the same cost categories in every channel's CAC (media, tools, the share of people's time), or comparisons between channels mislead.

sections.heading: Payback and LTV:CAC
sections.body:
**CAC payback (months)** = CAC ÷ (monthly revenue per customer × gross margin).

With CAC $600, ARPA $50/month and an 80% gross margin, payback = 600 / (50 × 0.8) = **15 months**. Stripe's resources describe 12 months or less as healthy, and LTV:CAC of about 3:1 as a common benchmark. Treat both as conventions, not laws.

Use gross margin, not revenue. For AI products, inference cost can push margin well below typical SaaS levels, which lengthens payback.

sections.heading: What attribution can and cannot do
sections.body:
**Attribution** splits credit for a conversion among the touchpoints a user was seen to have. It does **not** show what would have happened without a channel.

Facts about GA4 (Google Analytics Help):
- For paid and organic channels, the options are **data-driven** (recommended) and **last click**. Last click ignores direct traffic.
- **First click, linear, time decay and position-based were removed in November 2023.**
- Changing the model applies to historical and future data, and only to event-scoped traffic dimensions.
- Data-driven attribution can split credit into fractional conversions.

Typical blind spots:
- **Last click over-credits bottom-of-funnel channels** such as brand search and retargeting. These often reach people who were already going to buy.
- Touchpoints you can't track (podcasts, word of mouth, dark social, blocked cookies) get no credit.
- Data-driven models are still built from observed paths, not from experiments.

sections.heading: Incrementality
sections.body:
**Incrementality** asks: how many conversions happened *because of* this channel? You answer it with an experiment:

- **Holdouts**: withhold a campaign or retargeting from a random slice of users and compare conversion rates.
- **Geo experiments**: assign separate, non-overlapping regions at random to treatment (ads on) or control (ads off), then compare outcomes. Google researchers (Vaver and Koehler, 2011) describe this as a simple, systematic way to measure ad effectiveness.
- **Spend on/off or step tests** for channels you can't randomise by user.

Compute **incremental CAC** = spend ÷ incremental customers. It is often much higher than the attributed CAC for retargeting and brand search, and sometimes lower for upper-funnel channels that attribution under-credits.

keyPoints: Use CAC per channel; blended CAC hides expensive paid channels behind organic.
Payback = CAC / (monthly revenue × gross margin).
GA4 offers data-driven or last click; rule-based multi-touch models were removed in Nov 2023.
Attribution assigns credit; it does not measure causation.
Measure incrementality with holdouts or geo experiments and compute incremental CAC.

gotchas.trap: Our blended CAC is $200, so paid ads cost $200 per customer.
gotchas.correct: Compute paid CAC on paid-acquired customers only.

gotchas.trap: Retargeting has the lowest attributed CAC, so we should scale it.
gotchas.correct: Check incrementality with a holdout; retargeting often reaches people who would have bought anyway.

gotchas.trap: Switching GA4 to a linear model for a fairer view.
gotchas.correct: Linear was removed in Nov 2023; the options are data-driven and last click.

lessons.lab: Given monthly spend and new customers by channel, compute blended CAC, per-channel CAC and payback. Then design a 4-week holdout for retargeting: the randomisation unit, the holdout share, the primary metric, and how to compute incremental CAC.

lessons.title: Pricing models, packaging and value metrics
lessons.summary: How per-seat, usage-based, tiered, freemium and free-trial models work, how to pick a value metric that grows with customer value, and why AI inference costs push many products toward hybrid pricing.

sections.heading: Start from the value metric
sections.body:
A **value metric** is the unit you charge for: seats, API calls, documents processed, tracked events, active projects. A good one has three properties:

1. **It grows as the customer gets more value.** A customer who gets twice the benefit should usually pay more.
2. **The customer can understand and predict it.** If nobody can estimate next month's bill, procurement will push back.
3. **It tracks your costs well enough.** If one customer can drive your costs up 10x without paying more, the pricing will eventually eat your margin.

Pick the value metric before you pick numbers. Most pricing mistakes are a wrong unit, not a wrong price.

sections.heading: Per seat
sections.body:
**Per-seat** pricing charges for each user. It is simple to understand, easy to forecast and fits tools where value really scales with the number of people using them (for example a design tool where every seat is a working designer).

Its trap: in **collaborative** products, a seat price makes customers ration access. Teams share logins or stop inviting colleagues, which hurts the very network effect the product depends on. Common fixes are free viewer or guest roles, charging only for creators, or moving to an account-level or usage metric.

Seat pricing also fits poorly when one user can drive very different amounts of cost, which is common in AI products.

sections.heading: Usage-based and hybrid
sections.body:
**Usage-based** pricing charges for consumption (tokens, minutes, API calls, GB). Price tracks value and cost closely, and small customers can start cheaply. The downsides are **bill unpredictability** for customers and **revenue volatility** for you.

Many products use a **hybrid**: a platform fee or plan that includes an allowance, plus overage or credits beyond it. This gives customers a predictable base and protects you when usage spikes.

On Stripe, Stripe's docs now describe **Metronome** (now part of Stripe) as the primary usage-based billing platform and the recommended starting point for **new** integrations. The **Meters API** ("basic usage-based billing") remains supported for existing integrations. Check the current docs before you design a new integration.

sections.heading: Tiers and packaging
Freemium vs free trial
sections.body:
- **Freemium** gives a permanently free plan with limits. It works when the marginal cost of a free user is low and free users create value (word of mouth, content, network effects).
- A **free trial** gives full or near-full access for a limited time. It works when value is visible quickly and the product is expensive to serve.

For AI products every free request costs real inference money, so an unlimited free tier can burn cash with no path to revenue. Common responses are tight usage caps on the free plan, a time-limited trial, or a small credit allowance. Measure free-to-paid conversion **and** the cost of the free cohort, not conversion alone.

keyPoints: Choose the value metric first: it should grow with customer value, be predictable and track your costs.
Per-seat pricing is simple but can suppress adoption in collaborative products.
Usage-based pricing tracks value and cost but makes bills less predictable; hybrid plans with allowances are a common compromise.
Stripe recommends Metronome for new usage-based integrations; the Meters API stays supported.
Freemium needs a low marginal cost per free user; AI inference costs often favour trials or capped free plans.

gotchas.trap: Price a high-inference AI feature per seat with unlimited use, because seats are easy to forecast.
gotchas.correct: Tie price at least partly to usage (allowance plus overage, or credits) so heavy users cannot push margin negative.

gotchas.trap: Launch an unlimited free tier for an AI product and judge success only by sign-ups.
gotchas.correct: Cap free usage or use a time-limited trial, and track the inference cost of free users alongside conversion.

gotchas.trap: Build a brand-new usage-based integration on the Meters API without checking current guidance.
gotchas.correct: Stripe's docs recommend Metronome as the starting point for new usage-based integrations; the Meters API remains for existing ones.

lessons.lab: Take a product you know (or an imaginary AI writing assistant). List three candidate value metrics. For each, score 1-5 on 'grows with value', 'customer can predict it' and 'tracks our cost'. Pick one, then sketch a three-tier package with a free option or trial, and write one sentence on what triggers each upgrade.

lessons.title: Unit economics and revenue retention
lessons.summary: Gross margin when AI inference is a cost of goods sold, CAC payback, simple LTV and LTV:CAC, and the churn and retention metrics (logo churn, contraction, expansion, GRR and NRR) that show whether revenue compounds.

sections.heading: Gross margin with inference costs
sections.body:
**Gross margin = (revenue − cost of goods sold) / revenue.** COGS is the cost of *delivering* the product: production hosting, third-party services used per customer, and for AI products **model inference** (API spend or GPU time). Marketing spend belongs in CAC and new-feature engineering in R&D, not COGS.

Worked example (course numbers): a plan costs **$20/month**; the average customer drives **$6** of inference and **$2** of other delivery costs. Gross margin = (20 − 8) / 20 = **60%**. A classic SaaS product with little per-request cost often runs much higher, so AI products have less margin to pay back acquisition costs.

Inference cost is per customer and **skewed**: a few heavy users can cost far more than the average. Look at the margin distribution by customer, not just the blended average.

sections.heading: CAC and payback
sections.body:
**Customer acquisition cost (CAC)** = sales and marketing spend in a period / new customers acquired in that period.

**CAC payback (months) = CAC / (monthly revenue per customer × gross margin).** Use gross-margin-adjusted revenue: only the margin repays acquisition. (Stripe states it as CAC / monthly profit per customer, where profit is revenue minus the costs of serving that customer; revenue × gross margin is the usual way to get that figure.)

Worked example: CAC **$600**, ARPA **$50/month**, gross margin **80%** → 600 / (50 × 0.8) = **15 months**. Stripe's resources describe payback of about 12 months or less as healthy. Treat that as a common convention, not a law; it depends on your churn and cash position.

sections.heading: LTV and LTV to CAC
sections.body:
A simple **lifetime value** for a subscription business: **LTV = ARPA × gross margin / monthly churn rate**. With $50 ARPA, 80% margin and 3% monthly churn: 50 × 0.8 / 0.03 ≈ **$1,333**.

**LTV:CAC** compares that value with the cost to acquire it. A ratio around **3:1** is a widely quoted convention. Be careful:

- LTV is very sensitive to the churn estimate. Young cohorts make churn look lower than it is.
- Using revenue instead of gross margin overstates LTV, badly so for AI products.
- A high ratio with a very long payback can still run you out of cash.

sections.heading: Churn types
sections.body:
- **Logo (customer) churn**: share of customers who cancel.
- **Revenue churn**: MRR lost to cancellations.
- **Contraction**: MRR lost from customers who stay but downgrade or use less.
- **Expansion**: extra MRR from existing customers (upgrades, more seats, more usage).

Logo and revenue churn can tell different stories: losing many small customers can be a high logo churn with low revenue churn, and losing one large account the opposite. Also separate **voluntary** churn (the customer decided to leave) from **involuntary** churn (a failed payment), because the fixes are different.

sections.heading: GRR and NRR
sections.body:
For a cohort of customers that existed at the start of the period:

- **NRR = (starting MRR − churn − contraction + expansion) / starting MRR**
- **GRR = (starting MRR − churn − contraction) / starting MRR**

GRR excludes expansion, so it **cannot exceed 100%**. NRR above 100% means the existing base grows even with no new customers.

Worked example: starting MRR $200k, churn $10k, contraction $6k, expansion $26k → NRR = 210 / 200 = **105%**, GRR = 184 / 200 = **92%**. New-customer MRR is never part of either metric.

keyPoints: For AI products, inference is COGS; gross margin = (revenue − COGS) / revenue.
CAC payback = CAC / (monthly revenue per customer × gross margin).
Simple LTV = ARPA × gross margin / monthly churn; LTV:CAC of about 3:1 is a convention, not a rule.
Track logo churn, revenue churn, contraction and expansion separately.
GRR excludes expansion and is capped at 100%; NRR includes expansion and can exceed 100%; neither includes new customers.

gotchas.trap: Compute CAC payback with revenue instead of gross-margin-adjusted revenue.
gotchas.correct: Multiply monthly revenue by gross margin first; only the margin repays acquisition cost.

gotchas.trap: Report GRR of 108% because expansion was strong.
gotchas.correct: GRR excludes expansion and cannot exceed 100%. Strong expansion shows up in NRR.

gotchas.trap: Include new customers' MRR in the NRR numerator.
gotchas.correct: NRR and GRR measure only the cohort that existed at the start of the period.

lessons.lab: In a spreadsheet or the course SQL runner, build a 12-month MRR table for 20 made-up customers with starting MRR, churn, contraction and expansion. Compute monthly GRR and NRR, then CAC payback and simple LTV for CAC $600, ARPA $50 and margins of 80% and 60%. Note how the AI-style 60% margin changes payback.

lessons.title: Billing implementation, tax and price changes
lessons.summary: Subscriptions and prorations on Stripe, billing mode, previewing invoices, taxes and merchant of record vs selling direct, and how to change and test prices without breaking trust.

sections.heading: Subscriptions and prorations
sections.body:
When a customer changes plan mid-period, Stripe can **prorate**. The `proration_behavior` parameter takes:

- `create_prorations` (default): create proration items that appear on the **next** invoice;
- `always_invoice`: create prorations and **invoice immediately**;
- `none`: no prorations.

Prorations are computed **to the second** by default. Example from the docs' logic: upgrading from $10 to $20 halfway through the period gives a −$5 credit for unused time and a +$10 charge for the rest of the period, a net **+$5**.

Other behaviours to know:

- **Negative prorations are not refunded automatically**; they stay as credit unless you refund.
- **Usage-based prices are not prorated.**
- To show the customer the amount before confirming, preview with **`invoices.create_preview`** and pass the same `proration_date` when you then update the subscription.

sections.heading: Billing mode
sections.body: Stripe subscriptions have a **billing mode**: `flexible` or `classic`. Flexible is the default for newer API versions (from `2025-09-30.clover`), requires at least `2025-06-30.basil`, and **cannot be reverted** to classic. Under flexible mode, proration credits are based on the price that was **actually billed**, which can change credit amounts compared with classic. Check the billing-mode page before relying on old proration examples.

sections.heading: Taxes and merchant of record
sections.body:
Selling software internationally means indirect taxes (VAT, GST, US sales tax): registering, calculating, collecting and filing.

- **Selling direct**: you are the merchant. With Stripe Billing plus a tax tool you still own registrations, filings and liability.
- **Merchant of record (MoR)**: another company is the legal seller to your customer and handles tax compliance. Stripe's own MoR product is **Managed Payments**: Stripe (via Link) is the merchant, the customer sees the purchase as sold through Link, and it covers indirect tax in many countries.

Trade-offs to check in the docs: Managed Payments charges a fee **on top of** standard processing; it is for **digital products**; it works through **Checkout or Payment Links** only and does **not support Connect**; and you give up some control (descriptor, refunds Stripe may issue). An MoR suits a small team selling digital products globally; selling direct suits teams that need full control, physical goods or marketplace flows.

sections.heading: Changing prices
Testing prices responsibly
sections.body:
Price tests are not ordinary UI tests:

- **Randomise by account (or by person for consumer apps) and keep assignment stable.** A visitor who sees $20 on Monday and $30 on Tuesday will lose trust. Flag systems that hash a stable key keep a user in the same variant; for B2B, use group (account) bucketing so a whole company sees one price.
- **Measure revenue, not just conversion.** A higher price can lower conversion and still raise revenue per visitor, and the full effect shows only after renewals and churn.
- **Size the test.** Price changes often move conversion by small amounts, which need large samples to detect.
- **Prefer lower-risk designs** when you can: test on new customers only, test packaging instead of headline price, or test by region with a consistent price inside each region.
- Honour any price a customer was shown when they buy.

keyPoints: proration_behavior: create_prorations (default, next invoice), always_invoice (bill now), none.
Negative prorations are not refunded automatically; usage-based prices are not prorated.
Preview the amount with invoices.create_preview and pass the same proration_date.
Flexible billing mode is the default on newer API versions and cannot be reverted.
A merchant of record handles indirect tax as the legal seller; Stripe's MoR is Managed Payments (digital products, Checkout or Payment Links, no Connect, extra fee).
Price tests need stable account-level assignment and revenue-based, longer-window metrics.

gotchas.trap: Expect a downgrade to trigger an automatic refund of the unused time.
gotchas.correct: Negative prorations become credit; refund explicitly if your policy promises it.

gotchas.trap: Show the customer an estimated upgrade price computed in your own code.
gotchas.correct: Preview with invoices.create_preview and reuse the same proration_date on the update so the numbers match.

gotchas.trap: Randomise a price test per page view.
gotchas.correct: Bucket on a stable user or account key so each customer always sees one price.

gotchas.trap: Choose Managed Payments for a Connect marketplace selling physical goods.
gotchas.correct: Managed Payments is for digital products, through Checkout or Payment Links, and does not support Connect.

lessons.lab: In Stripe test mode, create two monthly prices ($10 and $20) and a subscription on the first. Preview an upgrade with invoices.create_preview and a fixed proration_date, then apply it once with create_prorations and once (on a second subscription) with always_invoice. Compare the invoices and note where the net amount appears.
