Mixpanel defaults to Any Order, which lowers conversion.
Mixpanel treats the first step as an exclusion step by default.
Mixpanel's funnel window cannot exceed 24 hours.
questions.explanation: Mixpanel funnels default to a 7-day conversion window, configurable up to 366 days or 12 sessions. A 30-day SQL window admits late converters the report excludes. Align the window before comparing numbers.
rationales: Correct. The windows differ.
The default is Specific Order, and Any Order would not lower conversion.
An exclusion step cannot be the first or last step.
The window can be set up to 366 days.

questions.scenario: A funnel query joins all `checkout_started` rows to all `order_paid` rows on `user_id` where the paid time is later, then divides `count(*)` of the join by `count(*)` of checkout_started rows. Users who retry checkout often make the rate exceed 100%.
questions.stem: What is the root cause?
options: The join condition should use >= instead of >.
PostgreSQL evaluates count(*) before the join.
The query needs an ORDER BY to process events in time order.
Row fan-out: each start pairs with every later payment, so the numerator counts pairs, not users or attempts.
questions.explanation: A many-to-many join on user_id multiplies rows: three starts and two later payments make up to six pairs. Reduce each step to one row per user (or per attempt with a proper key) before joining, or count distinct users.
rationales: Changing the inequality barely changes the pair count.
Aggregates are computed after the join; that is why pairs are counted.
ORDER BY does not affect join cardinality.
Correct. Aggregate per user before the join.

questions.scenario: A daily dashboard tile shows the 7-day trial-to-paid funnel by entry date. The last six days always look much worse than earlier days, and every morning they "recover".
questions.stem: What is the best change?
options: Shorten the window to 1 day so all days are comparable.
Switch to Any Order so more users qualify.
Show only entry dates whose 7-day window has fully elapsed, or mark recent dates as incomplete.
Smooth the line with a 7-day moving average.
questions.explanation: Users who entered in the last six days have not had their full window to convert, so their conversion is censored. Reporting only closed windows, or clearly labelling open ones, keeps periods comparable.
rationales: This changes the metric to something else and still leaves today's entrants incomplete.
Order is not the issue; time is.
Correct. Compare only complete windows.
A moving average blends incomplete days into complete ones and hides the problem.

questions.scenario: You must rebuild in SQL a three-step funnel that a product tool computes with Specific Order and a 7-day conversion window, counting unique users.
questions.stem: Which two conditions must the SQL enforce? (Select two.)
options: Each step's timestamp is later than the same user's timestamp for the previous step.
Every step happens no later than 7 days after the user's step-1 time.
Steps 2 and 3 may happen in either order as long as both are within 7 days.
The numerator counts every step-3 event so repeat users are weighted more.
questions.explanation: Specific Order means each step must follow the previous one, and the conversion window bounds how long after entry users may complete the funnel. Unique counting means one count per user, not per event.
rationales: Correct. This is the ordering rule.
Correct. This is the window rule, anchored at entry.
That describes Any Order, not Specific Order.
That is Totals counting, not Uniques.

questions.scenario: For the same weekly cohort, one chart shows week-4 retention of 30% and another shows 18%. Both are computed correctly from the same data.
questions.stem: Which explanation is consistent with both numbers?
options: The 30% chart uses unbounded retention (active in week 4 or later); the 18% chart uses N-day retention (active in exactly week 4).
The 30% chart uses N-day retention; the 18% chart uses unbounded retention.
The 30% chart counts events instead of users.
One chart uses rolling weeks, which always gives exactly 12 points more.
questions.explanation: Unbounded retention counts anyone active in the bucket or any later one, so it is always at least as high as N-day retention for the same bucket. Mixpanel calls these "On or After" (default) and "On".
rationales: Correct. Unbounded >= N-day.
Reversed: unbounded cannot be lower than N-day.
The premise says both are correct user-based retention.
Rolling vs calendar changes buckets, but not by a fixed amount.

sources.title: Retention types — Amplitude Dashboard REST API

questions.scenario: Your SQL computes N-day weekly retention: the share of a cohort active in exactly week N. A teammate rebuilds the report in Mixpanel without touching the retention settings, and every week's number is higher than yours.
questions.stem: What should the teammate change to match your definition?
options: Switch from calendar to rolling buckets.
Change the retention criterion from the default "On or After" to "On".
Increase the conversion window to 30 days.
Change counting from Uniques to Totals.
questions.explanation: Mixpanel retention defaults to "On or After", which is unbounded: a user counts for week N if they return in that week or any later one. "On" counts only returns in exactly that bucket, which is N-day retention.
rationales: Bucket alignment matters, but it does not explain uniformly higher numbers.
Correct. That aligns the definitions.
Conversion windows belong to funnels, not retention buckets.
Totals would not produce a retention percentage that matches yours.

questions.scenario: A weekly retention table has 12 cohorts. The overview chart averages each column over all 12 cohorts, treating cells a cohort has not reached yet as 0. The averaged curve drops sharply after week 6, and leadership asks what broke in week 6.
questions.stem: What is the best response?
options: Investigate a week-6 product issue, since the curve clearly shows one.
Switch to unbounded retention, which removes the drop.
Recompute each column's average using only cohorts old enough to have that week; unreached cells are unknown, not zero.
Average rows instead of columns.
questions.explanation: Later columns include more young cohorts with no data yet, and counting them as zero pulls the average down. That is right-censoring, not user behaviour. Averaging only cohorts that have reached each week removes the artifact. Mixpanel does the same: its average retention counts only completed time periods, so newer cohorts do not drag later buckets down.
rationales: The drop is an artifact of the averaging, not evidence of a product problem.
Unbounded retention still has unreached cells, so the artifact remains.
Correct. Handle censored cells as missing.
Row averages answer a different question and do not fix the censoring.

questions.scenario: A user signs up at 23:00 and returns at 09:00 the next morning, 10 hours later. The team uses Mixpanel retention with daily buckets.
questions.stem: How is this return counted?
options: Day 1 in both rolling and calendar modes.
Day 1 in rolling mode and Day 0 in calendar mode.
Day 0 in rolling mode (it is within 24 hours of birth) and Day 1 in calendar mode.
It is not counted in either mode because it is under 24 hours.
questions.explanation: In Mixpanel's rolling mode, Day 1 is 24-48 hours after birth, so a return 10 hours later falls in Day 0. Calendar mode uses calendar days, so the next calendar day is Day 1.
rationales: Rolling mode measures elapsed hours, not dates.
Reversed.
Correct.
It is counted, in Day 0 under rolling mode.

questions.scenario: Two analysts compute "week-4 retention" for the same product and get different numbers. You are asked to write a definition that anyone can compute the same way.
questions.stem: Which two elements must the definition specify? (Select two.)
options: The cohort (birth) event and bucket size, e.g. users grouped by week of first signup_completed.
The return event that counts as retained, and whether week N is bounded (exactly week N) or unbounded (week N or later).
That total events per bucket are used so heavy users are represented.
That users inactive in week 0 are removed so the curve is not dominated by tourists.
questions.explanation: Retention depends on who is in the cohort, what counts as coming back, and whether buckets are bounded or unbounded. Tools expose these same choices, such as Mixpanel's "On" vs "On or After". Counting events or silently dropping users changes the metric into something else.
rationales: Correct. Without it, cohorts differ.
Correct. Without it, the numerator differs.
Retention is a share of users; counting events is a different metric.
Removing early churners is survivorship bias and inflates retention.

sources.title: Retention types — Amplitude Dashboard REST API

questions.scenario: Events for many users are in one table. You need to split each user's events into sessions, where a session ends after more than 30 minutes of inactivity.
questions.stem: Which approach is correct in PostgreSQL?
options: Group by user_id and date_trunc('hour', ts) and treat each group as a session.
Flag rows where ts minus lag(ts) over (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts) exceeds 30 minutes or is NULL, then take a running sum of the flags per user as the session number.
Use row_number() over (ORDER BY ts) and start a new session every 30 rows.
Use lag(ts) OVER (ORDER BY ts) without a partition, since timestamps are already sorted.
questions.explanation: Sessionization is a gap rule per user: lag gives the previous event's time within the user's partition, the flag marks session starts, and a running sum turns the flags into session ids. The first event has a NULL lag and correctly starts session 1.
rationales: Hour buckets split sessions that cross the hour boundary and merge separate sessions inside one hour.
Correct. This is the standard flag-and-sum pattern.
Row counts have nothing to do with inactivity gaps.
Without PARTITION BY, the gap is measured to another user's event.

questions.scenario: An engineer wants the first event per user and writes `SELECT * FROM events WHERE row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts) = 1;`. Postgres rejects it.
questions.stem: What is the correct fix?
options: Move the condition to HAVING.
Compute row_number() in a CTE or subquery, then filter rn = 1 in the outer query.
Add GROUP BY user_id so the window function is allowed in WHERE.
Replace row_number() with rank(), which is allowed in WHERE.
questions.explanation: Window functions are evaluated after WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING, so they cannot appear in those clauses. Computing the row number in a subquery or CTE and filtering outside is the standard approach.
rationales: HAVING also runs before window functions.
Correct.
Grouping does not make window functions usable in WHERE.
No window function is allowed in WHERE.

sources.title: Value expressions (FILTER, window calls) — PostgreSQL docs

questions.scenario: To tag each event with the user's most recent plan, a query uses `last_value(plan) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts)`. Every row just shows its own plan.
questions.stem: Why, and what is the fix?
options: last_value ignores ORDER BY; sort the table first.
With ORDER BY, the default frame ends at the current row (and its peers); specify ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING.
last_value only works without PARTITION BY; remove it.
The plan column needs an index for last_value to read later rows.
questions.explanation: In PostgreSQL, when ORDER BY is present the default frame runs from the partition start through the current row and its peers. So last_value sees only up to the current row. Widening the frame, or using first_value with descending order, returns the partition's last value.
rationales: ORDER BY inside OVER does control ordering; the frame is the issue.
Correct.
Removing the partition would mix users.
Indexes do not change query semantics.

sources.title: Value expressions (FILTER, window calls) — PostgreSQL docs

questions.scenario: A streak query computes `ts::date - row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts)` directly on the raw events table and groups by the result. Users who are active several times a day show many short streaks instead of one long one.
questions.stem: What is the fix?
options: First reduce to one row per user per day (SELECT DISTINCT user_id, ts::date) and apply row_number() to those days.
Order by ts DESC instead.
Group by date_trunc('week', ts) instead of the computed value.
Replace row_number() with lag().
questions.explanation: Gaps-and-islands needs one row per user per day, so that consecutive days give a constant date minus row number. Several events on one day get different row numbers and split one day across islands. Deduplicating to distinct user-days first fixes it.
rationales: Correct. Each day then counts once.
Reversing order does not remove the duplicate-day problem.
Weekly grouping changes the question and loses daily streaks.
lag alone does not identify islands without further steps.

questions.scenario: A "median time between purchases" metric is computed with `ts - lag(ts) OVER (ORDER BY ts)` on the purchases table. The median comes out at a few seconds.
questions.stem: What is wrong?
options: lag needs an explicit offset of 1.
lead should be used instead of lag.
Medians cannot be computed over intervals.
The window has no PARTITION BY user_id, so gaps are measured between different users' purchases.
questions.explanation: Without a partition, the previous row is whichever purchase happened just before, by any user, so gaps shrink with total volume. Partitioning by user_id measures each customer's own time between purchases.
rationales: The default offset is already 1.
lead gives the same gaps, shifted, and has the same partition problem.
Interval medians can be computed, e.g. with percentile_cont on epoch seconds.
Correct.

questions.scenario: A running count uses `count(*) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts)`. Several events share identical timestamps and get the same running count.
questions.stem: Which two statements about PostgreSQL window frames are true? (Select two.)
options: When ORDER BY is present, the default frame runs from the partition start through the current row plus any peers with an equal sort key.
When ORDER BY is omitted, the default frame is the whole partition.
The default frame is ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW.
The default frame excludes peers, so tied rows always get different counts.
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL's default frame with ORDER BY is RANGE-based through the current row's last peer, which is why tied timestamps share a running count. Without ORDER BY, every row sees the whole partition. A ROWS frame plus a unique tie-breaker gives strict row-by-row counts.
rationales: Correct. That explains the tied counts.
Correct.
That is not the default.
Peers are included, which is the observed behaviour.

questions.scenario: Signup conversion by flow: Desktop A 400/1,000 (40%), B 90/200 (45%). Mobile A 20/200 (10%), B 120/1,000 (12%). Overall A 35%, B 17.5%. Traffic was meant to split evenly by platform.
questions.stem: What is the best conclusion?
options: Flow B is worse; the overall number is what matters to the business.
This is Simpson's paradox: B wins in both segments but got mostly mobile traffic. Compare within segments and investigate why the platform mix differs between flows.
The segments are too small to read; use the overall rate only.
Average the two segment rates per flow without weights and pick the higher one.
questions.explanation: B converts better on both desktop and mobile, but most of its traffic came from mobile, which converts worse for both flows, so its total is lower. The mix difference is the real finding and may point to a ramp or assignment bug. Within-segment comparisons, or a common weighting, give the fair answer.
rationales: The overall gap is driven by mix, not by the flow.
Correct.
Hundreds of users per cell is enough to see the pattern; ignoring segments hides it.
An unweighted average happens to favour B here, but it skips the important question of why the mix differs.

questions.scenario: Three months after a price increase, a PM runs an in-app survey: 92% of respondents say the new price is fair. The PM concludes the increase did not hurt customer sentiment.
questions.stem: What is the main flaw?
options: Survivorship bias: only customers who stayed can answer an in-app survey, so those who left over price are missing.
Simpson's paradox between monthly and annual plans.
The survey should have used a 7-point scale.
Three months is too short for any survey.
questions.explanation: Respondents are the customers who survived the change. Those most upset by the price likely churned and cannot answer. Judge the change on the full pre-change cohort: churn, downgrade and conversion rates, plus exit feedback.
rationales: Correct.
Nothing suggests a mix reversal; the sample is missing people.
Scale design does not fix who is missing.
Timing is not the core problem.

questions.scenario: Users who connect the Slack integration have twice the 90-day retention of those who do not. A PM proposes forcing Slack connection during onboarding to double retention.
questions.stem: What is the best response?
options: Ship it; a 2x gap is too large to be noise.
Treat it as a hypothesis: adopters self-select and were likely more engaged already. Test with an experiment, or at least compare pre-adoption engagement.
Segment further until a group without the gap appears.
Use unbounded retention to confirm the effect.
questions.explanation: Adopters choose to adopt, so the comparison mixes the feature's effect with who chooses it. Only randomization isolates the causal effect. Pre-adoption comparisons can show how much of the gap existed before adoption.
rationales: A large gap can be entirely selection.
Correct.
Slicing until a pattern appears is a fishing exercise.
Changing the retention definition does not address selection.

questions.scenario: After launching a new onboarding checklist, an analyst reports that "users with 3+ sessions in week 1" retain worse than before the launch, and recommends rolling back. The checklist roughly doubled how many users reach 3 sessions in week 1.
questions.stem: What is the problem with this analysis?
options: It should use median sessions instead of a 3-session threshold.

The segment is defined by behaviour the launch changed, so it now includes less-engaged users who previously would not qualify. Compare all signups before and after, or segment by pre-launch attributes.
It should use N-day rather than unbounded retention.
The analysis is valid; rolling back is correct.
questions.explanation: Segmenting on a post-change behaviour changes who is in the segment, so before and after groups are not alike. The fair comparison uses the whole signup cohort, or segments fixed before exposure such as platform or acquisition channel.
rationales: A different threshold still conditions on something the change affects.
Correct.
The retention definition is not the flaw.
The comparison is confounded by segment composition.

questions.scenario: Your team is about to break down a launch's conversion results by platform, country, plan and acquisition channel.
questions.stem: Which two practices reduce the risk of misleading conclusions? (Select two.)
options: Report each segment's size and mix alongside its rate.
Choose the key segments in advance and define them by attributes fixed before the launch.
Keep slicing until a segment shows a significant effect, then report that segment.
Silently drop small segments so the table looks cleaner.
questions.explanation: Sizes and mix reveal Simpson-style reversals and tiny-sample noise. Pre-chosen, pre-launch segments avoid fishing and composition changes. Slicing until something looks significant produces chance findings.
rationales: Correct.
Correct.
This is p-hacking by segmentation.
Hiding segments hides mix effects and data problems.

questions.scenario: Daily signups jumped 35% overnight on a Tuesday. The growth channel celebrates. The same morning, mobile shipped a new analytics SDK version.
questions.stem: What should the dashboard owner do first?
options: Attribute the jump to the latest campaign and increase its budget.
Check data-quality signals for the SDK change (duplicates, new event names, identity changes) and annotate the release on the chart.
Remove the Tuesday data point as an outlier.
Switch the chart to a 28-day moving average.
questions.explanation: Sudden steps often come from instrumentation changes, not behaviour. Checking data quality before the business metric, and annotating releases and tracking changes, prevents false wins and lets readers interpret the chart later.
rationales: This acts on an unverified change.
Correct.
Deleting data hides whatever happened.
Smoothing hides the step without explaining it.

sources.title: STEDII properties of a good metric — Microsoft ExP

questions.scenario: Every Monday morning, the weekly active users chart shows a steep drop in the latest week, and someone opens an incident. By Friday the drop has mostly disappeared.
questions.stem: What is the best fix?
options: Move the review to Friday.
Switch to daily active users.
Exclude the current partial week, or draw it distinctly (dashed or labelled to-date) so it is not compared with complete weeks.
Raise the alerting threshold so the drop does not page anyone.
questions.explanation: The latest week is incomplete, so its totals are lower by construction. Showing incomplete periods differently or excluding them stops a reporting artifact from looking like a behaviour change. The same applies to open funnel windows and unreached retention cells. Mixpanel, for example, marks incomplete retention buckets with an asterisk because that data is still in flux.
rationales: The week is still partial on Friday; the artifact only shrinks.
Daily charts have the same partial-day issue for today.
Correct.
This hides the symptom and also hides real drops.

questions.scenario: A startup's analytics dashboard has 40 charts. In a review, nobody can name a decision any chart has changed in the last quarter.
questions.stem: What is the best redesign approach?
options: Add filters to every chart so each team can explore more.
List the decisions the team makes regularly, keep one chart per question with a defined metric, owner and action threshold, and remove the rest.
Split the 40 charts into four tabs of 10.
Replace the charts with a single table of all metrics.
questions.explanation: Dashboards work when each chart answers a question tied to a decision. Metrics should be interpretable and actionable, as Microsoft ExP's STEDII properties put it. Charts nobody would act on add noise and hide the ones that matter.
rationales: More exploration does not create decisions.
Correct.
Reorganizing keeps the same unused charts.
A wall of numbers is harder to act on, not easier.

sources.title: STEDII properties of a good metric — Microsoft ExP

questions.scenario: A retention curve chart will be shared in a company-wide report. Some readers use screen readers.
questions.stem: Which approach best follows W3C WAI guidance for complex images?
options: Set the alt text to "chart".
Leave alt text empty, since the chart is decorative.
Rely on colour so each cohort line is easy to tell apart.
Give a short text alternative stating what the chart shows, plus a longer description such as a data table or a summary of the trend.
questions.explanation: W3C WAI treats charts as complex images that need a short alternative and a longer description conveying the same information, for example the underlying data. That also helps sighted readers check the numbers.
rationales: "chart" conveys none of the information.
A data chart is informative, not decorative.
Colour alone excludes colour-blind and screen-reader users.
Correct.

questions.scenario: You need, in one query over `events`, the number of distinct users who did `signup_completed` and the number who did `first_project_created`, per week.
questions.stem: Which PostgreSQL construct expresses this most directly?
options: Two separate queries joined with UNION ALL and pivoted in a spreadsheet.
GROUP BY event, then a CASE in ORDER BY.
A window function count(*) OVER (PARTITION BY event).
count(DISTINCT user_id) FILTER (WHERE event = 'signup_completed') and the same with FILTER for the second event, grouped by date_trunc('week', ts).
questions.explanation: The FILTER clause restricts which rows an aggregate sees, so one grouped query can return several conditional counts side by side. date_trunc buckets timestamps into weeks.
rationales: This works but is clumsy and moves logic out of SQL.
ORDER BY does not create separate columns.
A window count keeps every row and counts events, not distinct users per week.
Correct.

sources.title: Value expressions (FILTER, window calls) — PostgreSQL docs

questions.scenario: A product team wants to run a test on a redesigned onboarding flow. The PM proposes: "Let's ship it to half of new signups and see which metrics move."
questions.stem: Which hypothesis would best turn this into a test that can support a decision?
options: Because session recordings show users abandon at the workspace setup step, simplifying that step will raise 7-day activation for new signups by at least 2 pp without increasing support tickets or setup errors.
The new onboarding will improve user engagement.
We will track 40 onboarding metrics and ship if any of them improves significantly.
We will run the test until activation becomes significant, then ship.
questions.explanation: A useful hypothesis names the evidence, the change, the population, one primary metric with a minimum effect, and the guardrails. Vague or open-ended hypotheses invite picking metrics after the fact, and an open-ended run invites peeking. Microsoft ExP recommends defining OEC and guardrail metrics up front.
rationales: Correct. It fixes the population, primary metric, MDE and guardrails before launch.
Too vague. "Engagement" is not one measurable metric, and there is no effect size or guardrail.
Scanning 40 metrics makes a false positive very likely. With 40 independent metrics the family-wise error rate is far above 5%.
Running until significant is peeking and inflates the false-positive rate.

questions.scenario: A B2B collaboration tool wants to test a new shared-comment panel. Teammates in the same workspace see each other's comments. The team plans to randomise individual users with a PostHog feature flag.
questions.stem: What is the best randomisation choice?
options: Randomise individual users, because more units give more power.
Randomise by page view to get the most units.
Randomise by session so each user sees both versions and acts as their own control.
Randomise by workspace with a group-level flag, accept fewer units, and plan the sample size at the workspace level.
questions.explanation: When users in the same group affect each other, per-user randomisation lets the variants contaminate each other. Randomising the whole group contains the spillover. Evaluating the flag at the workspace level gives a whole account one variant, and Microsoft Research notes that tenant-level tests have fewer units and need care with power.
rationales: More units does not help when teammates in different arms affect each other. The estimate is biased.
Page-view randomisation has the same contamination problem, made worse.
Session-level randomisation shows a user both versions of a shared feature, which is confusing and contaminating.
Correct. Cluster randomisation contains interference, and power must be planned for the smaller number of clusters.

sources.title: Feature flag best practices — PostHog Docs

questions.scenario: A checkout redesign test uses "orders per visitor" as its primary metric.
questions.stem: Which of the following are appropriate guardrail metrics for this test? (Select two.)
options: Page load time on the checkout page
Orders per visitor, tracked again as a guardrail
Client crash or error rate during checkout
Whichever secondary metric shows the largest lift once the test ends
questions.explanation: Guardrail metrics are things that must not degrade, such as performance, crash rate and abandonment. Microsoft ExP lists page load time and crash rate as typical guardrails. The primary metric cannot also be its own guardrail, and choosing metrics after the test is cherry-picking.
rationales: Correct. Latency is a classic guardrail.
This is the primary metric. Listing it again adds no protection.
Correct. Crash and error rates are classic guardrails.
Choosing a metric after the test ends is cherry-picking, not a guardrail.

questions.scenario: An experiment scorecard has finished computing. The primary metric shows a significant 4% lift.
questions.stem: What should the analyst check first, before interpreting that lift?
options: Whether the lift is larger than last quarter's best experiment.
Data-quality metrics such as sample ratio mismatch and data loss.
The guardrail with the largest positive movement.
Whether the Bayesian chance to win is above 50%.
questions.explanation: Microsoft ExP recommends checking data-quality metrics such as SRM before reading the OEC. If the split or the logging is broken, the lift cannot be trusted. Comparisons with other experiments and with guardrails come afterwards.
rationales: Comparing with other experiments says nothing about whether this result is valid.
Correct. Check data quality first. An SRM invalidates the rest of the scorecard.
Guardrails are checked for regressions, and only after data quality.
A 50% chance to win is no evidence at all, and it is not a validity check.

questions.stem: A team planned a test to detect a 20% relative lift. Leadership now wants it to detect a 10% relative lift at the same baseline, alpha and power. Roughly how does the required sample size per arm change?
options: It halves.
It stays the same.
It roughly doubles.
It roughly quadruples.
questions.explanation: Sample size scales with variance divided by the squared effect (16σ²/d² in PostHog's rule of thumb). Halving d multiplies the required n by about 4.
rationales: Backwards. Smaller effects need more data.
Sample size depends strongly on the MDE.
The dependence is quadratic, not linear.
Correct. n ∝ 1/d², so halving d gives about 4x n.

sources.title: Sample size and running time — PostHog Experiments

questions.stem: Using PostHog's rule of thumb N = 16 × p(1-p) / d² per variant, what is N for a 10% baseline conversion rate and a 20% relative MDE?
questions.explanation: A 20% relative MDE on 10% is d = 0.02 absolute. 16 × 0.09 / 0.0004 = 3,600 per variant, which matches PostHog's documented example.
rationales: Off by a factor of 10.
Half the correct value, as if the constant were 8.
Double the correct value. The rule already gives a per-variant number.

sources.title: Sample size and running time — PostHog Experiments

questions.scenario: For a 10% → 12% test at α = 0.05 and 80% power, the exact two-sided formula with unpooled variances gives about 3,839 per arm. The 16σ²/d² rule gives 3,600.
questions.stem: What mainly explains why the rule of thumb gives the smaller number here?
options: The rule uses only the baseline variance p1(1-p1), and the treatment variance at 12% is larger than at 10%.
The exact formula is one-sided, so it needs more data.
The constant 16 is smaller than the exact constant 2(z₀.₉₇₅ + z₀.₈)².
The rule assumes 90% power instead of 80%.
questions.explanation: The exact formula sums p1(1-p1) + p2(1-p2) = 0.09 + 0.1056, and the rule uses 2 × 0.09. The exact constant is about 15.7, slightly less than 16, so the variance term explains the difference. When the treatment rate is closer to 50% than the baseline, the rule undercounts.
rationales: Correct. The treatment arm has variance 0.1056 vs 0.09, which the rule ignores.
The exact formula here is two-sided, and a one-sided test would need less data.
Backwards. 2 × (1.960 + 0.842)² ≈ 15.7, which is less than 16.
The rule is stated for 80% power and 95% confidence.

sources.title: Sample size and running time — PostHog Experiments

questions.scenario: An early-stage SaaS gets about 1,000 trial signups per arm per month. Trial-to-paid conversion is 5%. The founder wants to A/B test new copy on the pricing page that might lift conversion by 5% relative.
questions.stem: What is the best advice?
options: Run it, check weekly, and ship once p < 0.05.
Run it with α = 0.20 so it is more likely to reach significance.

At this traffic the detectable lift is about 55% relative, so a 5% lift cannot be detected. Test a bolder change, use a more sensitive upstream metric or variance reduction, or ship behind a flag with guardrails and qualitative research.
Split traffic into five copy variants so at least one is likely to win.
questions.explanation: With 1,000 users per arm at a 5% baseline, the MDE at α = 0.05 and 80% power is about 2.7 pp, or 55% relative. A 5% relative lift is far below that. The useful moves are larger changes, more sensitive metrics, variance reduction, or a non-experimental rollout.
rationales: Peeking at an underpowered test inflates false positives, and any "win" will exaggerate the effect.
Raising α after the fact just trades power for false positives and makes the result less trustworthy.
Correct. The test cannot detect the hoped-for effect, so change the design or the method.
More arms cut per-arm traffic, lower power further, and add multiple comparisons.

sources.title: Sample size and running time — PostHog Experiments

questions.stem: Traffic is fixed. Which actions can increase an experiment's power to detect the same true effect? (Select two.)
options: Apply CUPED using each user's pre-experiment value of the metric as a covariate.
Use a lower-variance metric that sits closer to the change and is a valid leading indicator of the goal.
Add three more treatment variants.
Check the results every day and stop at the first significant reading.
questions.explanation: Power rises when the variance of the effect estimate falls. CUPED removes variance explained by pre-experiment behaviour (about 50% on Bing), and a metric close to the change has less noise. More arms reduce per-arm sample size, and peeking raises false positives instead of power.
rationales: Correct. CUPED reduces variance, which works like adding traffic.
Correct. A more sensitive metric needs less data for the same effect.
Extra arms cut each arm's sample and reduce power.
Peeking inflates the false-positive rate. It does not add valid power.

sources.title: Sample size and running time — PostHog Experiments

questions.scenario: Control converts 400/4,000 and treatment 460/4,000. A two-proportion z-test gives p = 0.030 and a 95% CI for the difference of [0.14 pp, 2.86 pp].
questions.stem: Which interpretation is correct?
options: There is a 97% probability that the treatment is better than control.
The true relative lift is 15%.
The result is significant at the 5% level, and the data are consistent with true lifts from about 0.1 pp to 2.9 pp, so the true effect could be too small to matter.
There is a 3% probability that the null hypothesis is true.
questions.explanation: A frequentist p-value is the probability of data this extreme if there were no effect. It is not the probability that a hypothesis is true. The confidence interval shows the range of effects the data support. A lower bound near zero means the business value is uncertain even though the result is significant.
rationales: This is a Bayesian statement and does not follow from a frequentist p-value.
15% is the point estimate. The interval is wide.
Correct. Read significance together with the interval.
The p-value is not the probability that the null is true.

questions.scenario: A team runs fixed-horizon t-tests. The PM checks the dashboard every day and ends tests at the first day p < 0.05. Over a year, many "wins" fail to replicate.
questions.stem: What is the most likely cause, and what is the best fix?
options: Peeking inflates the false-positive rate well above 5%. Either analyse once at the planned sample size, or switch to a sequential method such as mSPRT that is valid under continuous monitoring.
The tests ran too long. Stop them even earlier.
Daily checks are fine, but the team should use a one-sided test.
The t-test is wrong for conversions. Using a chi-square test would fix the replication problem.
questions.explanation: Stopping at the first significant look turns a 5% test into a much higher error rate. In this course's A/A simulation, 10 looks gave about 20%. Always-valid sequential methods such as mSPRT, which Amplitude Experiment uses by default, allow monitoring without that inflation.
rationales: Correct. This names the cause and two valid fixes.
Stopping earlier makes the peeking problem worse.
A one-sided test does not fix repeated looks.
For two proportions the chi-square and z-tests agree. The problem is the stopping rule, not the test.

questions.scenario: An engineer new to Amplitude Experiment says: "Amplitude uses a plain t-test, so we must never look before the planned end date."
questions.stem: What is the most accurate response?
options: Correct. Amplitude only supports a pooled Student's t-test.
Amplitude corrects for peeking automatically whatever test you pick.
Amplitude uses a Bayesian engine only, so peeking never matters.
Amplitude Experiment uses sequential testing (mSPRT) by default, which gives always-valid results under monitoring. A Welch's T-test is an option, and if you choose it, peeking becomes a concern.
questions.explanation: Amplitude documents sequential testing (mSPRT) as the default, with a Welch's T-test as an option. Its own A/A simulation shows that the peeked T-test has a higher false-positive rate than mSPRT, so the protection depends on which method is chosen.
rationales: Wrong on both counts. The default is sequential, and the T-test option is Welch's.
There is no automatic peeking correction for the T-test option.
Amplitude's default is mSPRT, not Bayesian-only.
Correct. This matches Amplitude's documentation.

questions.scenario: An experiment scorecard reports 20 independent metrics, each tested at α = 0.05. The pre-registered primary metric is flat. One secondary metric is significant at p = 0.04, and the team wants to announce a win.
questions.stem: What is the best response?
options: Announce the win. p = 0.04 is below 0.05.
Drop the primary metric and make the significant metric primary from now on.

With 20 metrics, the chance of at least one false positive is about 64%. Judge on the primary metric, treat the secondary result as a hypothesis for a follow-up test, and apply a correction such as Bonferroni or BH to the family.
Rerun the analysis on a subset of users until the primary metric also becomes significant.
questions.explanation: 1 - 0.95^20 ≈ 0.64, so finding one significant metric out of 20 by chance is likely. The decision should rest on the pre-registered primary metric. Corrections such as Bonferroni (which Amplitude can apply) or Benjamini-Hochberg control error across the family.
rationales: This ignores multiple comparisons.
Switching the primary metric after seeing the results is cherry-picking.
Correct. Treat it as exploratory and correct for multiplicity.
Slicing until something is significant is p-hacking.

questions.stem: Ten metric p-values are [0.001, 0.008, 0.039, 0.041, 0.042, 0.06, 0.074, 0.205, 0.212, 0.216]. After the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure (scipy.stats.false_discovery_control) at q = 0.05, how many remain significant?
questions.explanation: The BH-adjusted values are [0.01, 0.04, 0.084, 0.084, 0.084, 0.1, ...]. Only the first two are at or below 0.05. Five raw p-values were below 0.05, which shows how much the correction matters.
rationales: The two smallest p-values survive BH.
Correct. The adjusted values are 0.01 and 0.04.
This counts raw p-values below 0.05 without correction.
Most of these are not significant even before correction.

questions.scenario: A team runs a PostHog experiment with six test variants plus control and eight secondary metrics. One variant beats control on one secondary metric.
questions.stem: What must the team keep in mind?
options: PostHog automatically applies Bonferroni across variants, so the result is already corrected.
PostHog limits experiments to one test variant, so the setup is invalid.
PostHog does not apply multiple-comparison correction across variants or metrics, so the team must account for the many comparisons themselves.
Bayesian results are never affected by multiple comparisons.
questions.explanation: PostHog's statistics docs say that no multiple-comparison correction is applied across variants or metrics, and its engine allows up to 19 test variants plus control. With 6 × 8 comparisons, a chance winner is likely unless the team adjusts.
rationales: PostHog does not apply automatic correction.
PostHog supports many variants, up to 19 plus control.
Correct. Correcting for multiplicity is the analyst's job here.
Looking at many comparisons and reporting the best one inflates false discoveries under any framework.

questions.scenario: A 50/50 test shows 50,500 users in control and 49,500 in treatment. A chi-square goodness-of-fit test gives p ≈ 0.0016. Treatment is winning on the primary metric.
questions.stem: What should the team do?
options: Ship. A 1% imbalance is negligible on 100,000 users.
Reweight the arms to 50/50 and report the adjusted lift.
Ignore the imbalance because treatment is winning anyway.
Treat it as a sample ratio mismatch: do not trust the results, and debug assignment, exposure logging and data processing before rerunning.
questions.explanation: A p-value of about 0.0016 against the planned split is a sample ratio mismatch. Microsoft ExP treats SRM as a sign of a bug that can bias every metric, because the missing users are not random. The fix is to find the cause, not to reweight.
rationales: At this sample size, a 1% imbalance is very unlikely to be chance.
Reweighting cannot recover users who are missing for non-random reasons.
A biased result can show a "win" that is not real.
Correct. Stop, diagnose and rerun.

sources.title: Diagnosing sample ratio mismatch — Microsoft Research
Online controlled experiments (encyclopedia entry) — Microsoft ExP

questions.scenario: A test has a significant sample ratio mismatch with fewer users than expected in treatment.
questions.stem: Which are plausible root causes? (Select two.)
options: The treatment page crashes on some older devices before the exposure event fires.
The planned sample size was set higher than necessary.
Treatment has a higher conversion rate than control.
The bot-filtering step in the pipeline flags more treatment traffic as bots because the new page triggers extra automated requests.
questions.explanation: Microsoft ExP's SRM taxonomy includes execution problems, such as crashes or redirects that lose users before logging, and log-processing problems, such as filtering that treats the arms differently. A difference in conversion or an oversized sample target does not change how many users are counted in each arm.
rationales: Correct. This is an execution-stage loss of exposures.
The target sample size does not affect the ratio between the arms.
Conversion differences are outcomes and do not change assignment counts.
Correct. This is a log-processing difference between the arms.

sources.title: Diagnosing sample ratio mismatch — Microsoft Research

questions.scenario: A redesigned home feed shows a +8% click-through lift in week one, +4% in week two, and +1% in week three.
questions.stem: What is the most likely explanation, and what should the team do?
options: A novelty effect. Look at the effect over time and for new users, run long enough for it to stabilise, and consider a long-term holdout.
A primacy effect. Ship immediately before it fades further.
Random noise. Average the three weeks and report +4.3%.
Seasonality. Ignore it, because A/B tests cancel seasonality out completely.
questions.explanation: An early lift that fades suggests users are clicking because the feed is new. Google's long-term study found that user learning takes a long time to converge, so short-term effects can mislead. Examining the trend and using a long-term holdout separates temporary effects from lasting ones.
rationales: Correct. This names the effect and gives sound next steps.
Primacy is an early drop that recovers. This is the opposite pattern.
A steady decline is a trend, not noise, and the average hides it.
Concurrent control handles shared seasonality, but it cannot explain a treatment effect that fades over time.

sources.title: Focus on the long term — Google Research

questions.scenario: A power-user tool moves its main toolbar. After 5 days, task completion is 3% lower in treatment. The design team is confident in the new layout from usability research.
questions.stem: What is the best next step?
options: Check for a primacy (change-aversion) effect: split results by new vs existing users and look at the daily trend. Keep the test running if guardrails allow.
Kill the change immediately. The data has spoken.
Restart the test with only users who liked the old toolbar.
Switch the primary metric to time on page, which is likely to look better.
questions.explanation: Experienced users often do worse at first with a changed layout, and then recover. New users have no habit to unlearn, so their result is a cleaner signal of the long-term effect. Short-term results can mislead about long-term outcomes, as Google's long-term study found.
rationales: Correct. Splitting by user tenure and looking at the trend reveals primacy.
Deciding after 5 days without checking for primacy risks killing a good change.
Selecting users by their attitudes biases the sample.
Changing the metric after the fact is cherry-picking.

sources.title: Focus on the long term — Google Research

questions.scenario: A signup-flow experiment uses a PostHog flag keyed on distinct ID. Some users see variant A before signup and variant B after they log in, and the funnel data looks inconsistent.
questions.stem: What is the cause, and what is the fix?
options: Flags are random on every request. Cache the value in localStorage.
PostHog flags cannot be used for experiments that span signup.
The rollout percentage was raised mid-test, which reshuffles all users.

Bucketing hashes the flag key with the distinct ID, which changes from anonymous to identified at signup. Use device bucketing, or call identify() before any flag is evaluated, so the user keeps one variant.
questions.explanation: PostHog assigns a bucket by hashing "{flag_key}.{distinct_id}". When an anonymous user becomes identified, the ID and therefore the bucket can change. Device bucketing hashes the stable $device_id instead, and calling identify() before flag evaluation avoids the switch. PostHog cautions against relying on experience continuity for this.
rationales: Assignment is deterministic, not random per request. Local caching is a workaround that does not address the cause.
PostHog documents ways to handle exactly this case.
Raising a rollout keeps earlier users included. It does not reshuffle them.
Correct. This matches PostHog's documented behaviour and fixes.

sources.title: Feature flag best practices — PostHog Docs

questions.scenario: A new search backend is behind a PostHog flag at 10% rollout with no problems. The team wants to raise it to 50%.
questions.stem: Which statement is correct?
options: Raising the rollout reshuffles everyone, so the original 10% may lose the feature.
Raising the rollout turns the rollout into a valid A/B test automatically.
The flag must be deleted and recreated to change the percentage.
Users already in the 10% stay included at 50%, because assignment is a deterministic hash compared with the rollout threshold.
questions.explanation: PostHog maps a hash of the flag key and distinct ID to a value in [0,1] and compares it with the rollout percentage, so raising the percentage only adds users. A rollout gives causal evidence only if you also keep and analyse a randomised control.
rationales: Hash-based assignment is stable, so earlier users are kept.
A rollout is not an experiment without a concurrent control and a planned analysis.
You can change rollout percentages in place.
Correct. This matches PostHog's documented behaviour.

sources.title: Feature flag best practices — PostHog Docs

questions.scenario: Legal requires a change to the consent banner in the EU. It will ship regardless of its effect on conversion. The team asks whether to A/B test it for four weeks first.
questions.stem: What is the best approach?
options: Ship through a staged feature-flag rollout while watching guardrails such as errors and latency, without treating the rollout as a causal experiment.
Run a four-week 50/50 A/B test and only ship if conversion does not drop.
Ship to everyone at once with no monitoring, because the change is mandatory.
Run a before/after comparison and present it as the causal impact of the change.
questions.explanation: When a change must ship anyway, an A/B test cannot change the decision. The real risk is breaking something, which a staged rollout with guardrail monitoring handles. Before/after comparisons are confounded by everything else that changed in the same period.
rationales: Correct. A staged rollout with guardrails fits a must-ship change.
The result cannot change the decision, and a four-week 50/50 test delays a legally required change for half of EU users.
Mandatory does not mean risk-free. Watch for breakage.
Before/after numbers are not causal evidence.

sources.title: Feature flag best practices — PostHog Docs

questions.stem: Which statements about PostHog Experiments are correct? (Select two.)
options: It offers a Bayesian engine (the default) and a frequentist engine.
It supports only a Bayesian engine.
It applies Bonferroni correction across all metrics automatically.
It supports up to 19 test variants plus a control.
questions.explanation: PostHog documents Bayesian (default) and frequentist statistics, and its experimentation engine supports up to 19 test variants plus control. It does not apply multiple-comparison correction, and it is not Bayesian-only.
rationales: Correct. Bayesian is the default, and frequentist is an option.
A frequentist engine is also available.
PostHog does not apply multiple-comparison correction.
Correct. Up to 19 test variants plus control.

questions.scenario: A hosted notebook product lets users publish notebooks as public pages. About 40% of new signups first land on someone else's public notebook from a search engine. Then they sign up and publish their own.
questions.stem: Which loop is this, and which input metric best tracks its health?
options: A content loop; track public, indexable notebooks published per new user and the visit-to-signup rate on those pages.
A paid loop; track cost per click on search ads.
A viral loop; track the number of email invites sent per user.
A sales-led loop; track qualified accounts handed to sales.
questions.explanation: Users create public pages, search brings visitors, and visitors become users who create more pages, so this is a content loop. Its inputs are pages created per user and how well those pages convert visitors. Choosing a few inputs the team can move follows the North Star input-metric approach.
rationales: Correct: user-generated public pages feed search traffic, which feeds new creators.
No ads are involved; traffic comes from organic search.
Nobody sends invites; the pages reach new people through search.
Nothing in the cycle depends on sales.

sources.title: North Star metric and inputs — Amplitude

questions.scenario: A team tracks referrals over a quarter. On average each activated user sends 3 invites, and 10% of invites turn into activated users. Assume this rate stays constant across generations.
questions.stem: If marketing brings in 1,000 activated users, about how many activated users will the company have in total from that seed, including all later generations of referrals?
options: About 1,430
Unlimited, because referrals keep compounding
questions.explanation: K = 3 × 0.10 = 0.3. With a steady K below 1, the geometric series gives 1/(1 − K) ≈ 1.43 users per seed user, so about 1,430 in total. A K below 1 still amplifies acquisition, but it does not grow without limit.
rationales: This counts only the first generation (300) and misses invites from invitees.
This multiplies by invites sent and ignores the 10% conversion.
Growth compounds without limit only when K is at least 1.

questions.scenario: A B2B tool reports a K-factor of 0.9. The figure is every signup that used a referral code divided by the number of users who sent at least one invite. Leadership wants to cut paid spend because "referrals almost sustain themselves".
questions.stem: Which two changes would give the most honest K before that decision? (Select two.)
options: Count only invitees who activate within a stated conversion window, and remove self-referrals and duplicate accounts.
Divide by all users who sent at least one invite in their lifetime, to smooth out monthly noise.
Run a holdout in which a random set of users never sees the referral prompt, to estimate how many referred signups are incremental.
Add organic signups from the same companies to the numerator, since they were probably influenced by referrals.
questions.explanation: An honest K counts activated invitees in a fixed window, removes gamed referrals, and checks how many referred users would have come anyway. Dividing only by users who invited inflates the per-user rate, and adding unattributed signups inflates it further. A funnel with an explicit conversion window and a randomised holdout address the two biggest biases.
rationales: Correct: this removes non-activated and gamed signups and bounds the time window.
The denominator should be all users in the cohort, not only lifetime inviters; this keeps the inflation.
Correct: a holdout measures the lift the referral programme actually causes.
This adds users with no evidence that referrals caused them, which inflates K.

sources.title: Tenant-randomized A/B tests — Microsoft Research ExP

questions.scenario: A team collaboration app tests a bigger referral reward. It randomises at the user level, 50/50. Treatment users invite teammates who sit in the same companies as control users, and many control users join shared workspaces with treatment users.
questions.stem: What is the main threat to this experiment's validity, and what is a better design?
options: Novelty effect; run the test for one more week.
Low power; add more variants to collect more data.
Sample ratio mismatch; rebalance traffic to 60/40.
Interference between groups; randomise at the workspace or company level instead.
questions.explanation: Users in different arms interact, so treatment changes the outcomes of control users and the comparison is biased. Randomising whole clusters, such as workspaces or tenants, keeps interactions within one arm. Microsoft ExP notes that tenant-level randomisation has its own challenges, such as fewer units and lower power.
rationales: Novelty is a time effect; it does not explain spillover between arms.
More variants spread traffic thinner and do nothing about interference.
Nothing suggests the split is wrong, and changing the ratio would not fix spillover.
Correct: spillover between connected users breaks independence; cluster-level randomisation contains it.

sources.title: Tenant-randomized A/B tests — Microsoft Research ExP

questions.scenario: Two candidate referral loops have the same yield, 0.5 new activated users per user per cycle. In Loop A an invite is usually accepted within 2 days. Loop B relies on a quarterly team-planning ritual, so a cycle takes about 90 days.
questions.stem: Over the next year, which statement is most accurate?
options: They contribute about the same, because K is equal.
Loop B contributes more, because a longer cycle means higher-intent invitees.
Loop A contributes much more, because its shorter cycle completes many more turns in the year.
You cannot compare them without knowing CAC.
questions.explanation: How much a loop contributes over a period depends on both yield and how many cycles complete in that period. A 2-day cycle can turn many times while a 90-day cycle turns about four times. That is why cycle time is a primary loop metric next to yield.
rationales: Equal yield per cycle does not mean equal output per year.
Invitee intent is not given, and the question states equal yield.
Correct: cycle time sets how many turns happen in the period.
CAC concerns paid acquisition, not how fast an organic loop compounds.

sources.title: North Star metric and inputs — Amplitude

questions.scenario: A developer-tools company has a free tier. Accounts that reach 10 active seats are flagged, a sales rep contacts them, and closed deals fund more reps and more free-tier marketing.
questions.stem: Which metric is the best input to monitor for this loop?
options: Qualified (10+ active seat) accounts created per month and their win rate.
Total registered free users.
Page views on the pricing page.
Number of emails sent by sales.
questions.explanation: This is a sales-led loop fed by product usage. Its yield depends on how many accounts reach the qualifying threshold and how many sales converts. Registered users and page views are vanity or distant proxies, and emails sent measures activity, not outcome.
rationales: Correct: qualified accounts and win rate are the loop's actual inputs and yield.
Total registrations include inactive users and are a vanity metric here.
Pricing page views are a weak, indirect signal.
Emails sent is activity, not an outcome.

sources.title: North Star metric and inputs — Amplitude

questions.scenario: An infrastructure product's onboarding funnel (signup, connect cloud account, first deploy) shows 22% conversion in Mixpanel with default settings. Interviews show many teams wait for a security review and deploy for the first time 9 to 14 days after signup.
questions.stem: What is the most likely problem with the 22% figure?
options: The funnel uses Any Order, so steps are counted out of order.
Mixpanel funnels cannot measure more than two steps.
The funnel counts Totals instead of Uniques.
The default 7-day conversion window cuts off users who activate after day 7, so activation is undercounted.
questions.explanation: Mixpanel funnels default to a 7-day conversion window, so first deploys on days 9 to 14 are not counted as conversions. Set the window to match real setup time, and keep it fixed when you compare periods. Step order defaults to Specific Order, and funnels support many steps.
rationales: The default step order is Specific Order, not Any Order.
Funnels support more than two steps.
Nothing indicates the counting mode was changed; Uniques would not explain a timing gap.
Correct: the 7-day default window excludes the slow but real activations.

questions.scenario: A B2B SaaS app gets about 2,000 signups a month. Its activation rate (first report shared within 14 days) is 5%. The team plans a one-month A/B test of a new onboarding checklist, about 1,000 users per arm, hoping for a 10% relative lift.
questions.stem: Which two actions are most sensible? (Select two.)
options: Run the test as planned and stop early as soon as the p-value drops below 0.05.
Recognise the test can only detect a very large lift (around 55% relative at this size), so test a bolder change or plan a longer run.
Use a more frequent, earlier metric (such as checklist step completion) as the primary metric, and keep 14-day activation and retention as guardrails.
Split the traffic across five checklist variants to learn more from one test.
questions.explanation: With 1,000 users per arm and a 5% baseline, the minimum detectable effect at 80% power and 95% confidence is about 2.7 percentage points, roughly 55% relative, far above a 10% lift. Bolder changes, longer runs and more sensitive upstream metrics are the practical responses. Stopping when the result looks significant inflates false positives, and more variants reduce power further.
rationales: Peeking and stopping early inflates the false-positive rate.
Correct: the test is badly underpowered for a 10% lift.
Correct: a more sensitive metric with outcome guardrails makes the test detect something useful.
Five variants split 2,000 users into very small arms, which makes power worse.

sources.title: Sample size and running time — PostHog Docs
STEDII properties of a good metric — Microsoft ExP

questions.scenario: Analysis shows that users who invite a teammate in week one retain twice as well at day 60. A PM proposes making "invite a teammate" a required onboarding step before users can reach the product.
questions.stem: What is the best response?
options: Ship it; the data proves inviting causes retention.
Ship it, and measure success by the share of users who invite in week one.
Test it as an experiment with day-60 retention as the key outcome, because the link may be correlational and forcing the step can game the activation metric.
Reject it; activation metrics should never involve other users.
questions.explanation: Users who invite may be the ones who already planned to adopt, so the retention gap does not show causation. A mandatory step raises the invite rate by definition while it may lower overall activation, which is Goodhart's law. An experiment judged on retention answers the real question.
rationales: The observed gap is correlational and could reflect selection.
Measuring the forced action guarantees a "win" that says nothing about retention.
Correct: validate causally and judge the change on the outcome you care about.
Team-based actions can be good activation events; the problem is forcing the step and calling it causal.

questions.scenario: A redesigned onboarding flow lifted week-one activation by 18% in an A/B test that ran 7 days. The team wants to report the full 18% as the expected long-term gain.
questions.stem: What should they do first?
options: Keep measuring the cohorts (for example 30- and 60-day retention), because early lifts can reflect novelty or learning effects that fade.
Report the 18%; a significant result is final.
Rerun the test with a 1-day duration to confirm it quickly.
Switch to a Bayesian analysis to remove novelty effects.
questions.explanation: Short tests can mislead about long-term effects. Google's long-term study found that user learning can take a long time to converge. Following retention cohorts beyond the first week shows whether the gain lasts.
rationales: Correct: longer-window outcomes show whether the lift is durable.
Statistical significance in week one says nothing about whether the effect lasts.
A shorter test makes novelty bias worse.
Changing the statistical method doesn't change how users behave over time.

sources.title: Focus on the long term — Google Research

questions.stem: A docs site's field data at the 75th percentile on mobile shows LCP 2.3 s, INP 240 ms and CLS 0.05. Which statement is correct under the web.dev "good" thresholds?
options: All three Core Web Vitals are good.
LCP fails because the threshold is 2.0 s.
LCP and CLS are good; INP is above the 200 ms "good" threshold.
CLS fails because the threshold is 0.01.
questions.explanation: The good thresholds are LCP ≤ 2.5 s, INP ≤ 200 ms and CLS ≤ 0.1, assessed at the 75th percentile. At 240 ms, INP misses its threshold while the other two pass.
rationales: INP at 240 ms is above 200 ms.
The LCP good threshold is 2.5 s.
Correct: only INP misses its threshold.
The CLS good threshold is 0.1.

questions.scenario: A team reports to leadership that the marketing site "passes Core Web Vitals". The evidence is a single Lighthouse run on a developer's laptop, and the dashboard still shows FID.
questions.stem: What is wrong with this report?
options: Nothing; Lighthouse is the official Core Web Vitals assessment.
FID is still the responsiveness metric, but it must be measured on mobile only.
Core Web Vitals use the median of field data, so they need more lab runs.
Core Web Vitals are assessed on real-user data at the 75th percentile, split by mobile and desktop, and INP replaced FID in 2024.
questions.explanation: web.dev defines the Core Web Vitals assessment at the 75th percentile of page loads, segmented by mobile and desktop. One lab run on a fast machine is not that. INP replaced FID as the responsiveness metric in 2024, so the dashboard is outdated too.
rationales: A single lab run is a diagnostic, not the field-data assessment.
FID was replaced by INP.
The assessment uses the 75th percentile, not the median.
Correct: the report uses the wrong data and a retired metric.

questions.scenario: A startup built its documentation as a client-side-rendered single-page app. The HTML shell is empty until a large JavaScript bundle loads and fetches content. Many docs pages get little organic traffic despite good content.
questions.stem: Which change is most likely to help both search visibility and loading performance?
options: Add more keywords to the page titles and keep client-side rendering.
Block the JavaScript bundle in robots.txt so crawlers read the shell faster.
Serve the docs as static or server-rendered HTML, so content is present in the initial response and less JavaScript is required.
Increase the sitemap <priority> of every docs page to 1.0.
questions.explanation: web.dev notes that crawlers can run JavaScript but often have rendering limits, and that server rendering delivers complete-looking pages. Static rendering also gives a consistently fast TTFB, and it suits docs whose URLs are known ahead of time. Shipping less JavaScript also improves responsiveness. Google Search Central adds that server-side or pre-rendering is still a great idea, and that Google won't render JavaScript from files blocked in robots.txt.
rationales: Keywords don't help if the content isn't reliably rendered.
Blocking the JavaScript would stop crawlers from rendering content at all.
Correct: content in the initial HTML is easier to index and faster to show.
Sitemap priority values don't fix rendering, and Google ignores them.

sources.title: JavaScript SEO basics — Google Search Central

questions.scenario: A growth team publishes integration guides. Leadership wants to judge the content programme by total pageviews and the number of keywords ranked.
questions.stem: Which measure better shows whether content works as an acquisition channel?
options: Signups and activated users from visitors who landed on each guide group, plus the visit-to-activation rate.
Total pageviews across all guides.
Average time on page.
Number of guides published per month.
questions.explanation: A channel matters when its visitors become activated users. Pageviews, time on page and output counts can rise while nobody signs up, which makes them vanity metrics for this decision. A metric the team can act on links the content to downstream activation.
rationales: Correct: it ties content to activation, the outcome that matters.
Pageviews can grow with irrelevant traffic.
Time on page is ambiguous: long can mean engaged or confused.
Output volume measures effort, not results.

sources.title: STEDII properties of a good metric — Microsoft ExP

questions.stem: A marketer wants to switch a GA4 property to the linear attribution model to give every touchpoint equal credit. What should you tell them?
options: Linear is available under Admin for paid and organic channels.
Linear is available only for Google paid channels.
Linear is the default, so no change is needed.
Linear, first click, time decay and position-based models were removed in November 2023; the options are data-driven or last click.
questions.explanation: Google Analytics Help states that first click, linear, time decay and position-based models are no longer available as of November 2023. For paid and organic channels, the choices are data-driven (recommended) and last click.
rationales: Linear is no longer available.
The Google paid channels option is last click, not linear.
Linear is neither the default nor available.
Correct: the rule-based multi-touch models were removed.

questions.scenario: In last-click attribution, retargeting ads show a CAC of $90, compared with $400 for paid social. The CFO proposes moving most of the paid social budget into retargeting.
questions.stem: What is the best next step?
options: Move the budget; last-click CAC is the most precise measure of channel efficiency.
Switch to data-driven attribution and move the budget if retargeting still looks cheapest.
Run an incrementality test, such as a randomised holdout or a geo experiment for retargeting, and compare incremental CAC across channels.
Cut both channels and rely on organic, because attribution cannot be trusted.
questions.explanation: Attribution assigns credit among observed touchpoints but does not show what would have happened without the channel. Retargeting often reaches people who were already likely to buy, so its attributed CAC can be far below its incremental CAC. Holdouts and geo experiments, which assign regions to treatment and control at random, measure causal lift.
rationales: Last click over-credits bottom-of-funnel channels.
Data-driven attribution is still built from observed paths, not experiments.
Correct: an experiment measures the conversions the channel actually causes.
Cutting both channels throws away the information you need; measure first.

sources.title: Geo experiments for ad effectiveness — Google Research

questions.scenario: Last month a SaaS company spent $30,000 on paid ads and acquired 50 customers from them. Another 100 customers arrived organically. Average revenue is $50 per customer per month at an 80% gross margin.
questions.stem: What is the CAC payback period for the paid channel?
options: 5 months
12 months
15 months
18.75 months
questions.explanation: Paid CAC = $30,000 / 50 = $600, and payback = CAC / (monthly revenue × gross margin) = 600 / (50 × 0.8) = 15 months. The blended CAC of $200 would wrongly suggest 5 months, because it counts organic customers that the spend did not buy.
rationales: This uses the blended CAC ($200), which includes organic customers.
This ignores gross margin (600 / 50).
Correct: $600 / $40 per month = 15 months.
This applies the 80% margin twice: 600 / (50 × 0.8 × 0.8) = 18.75.

questions.stem: Which two statements about GA4 attribution settings are accurate according to Google Analytics Help? (Select two.)
options: Data-driven attribution measures each channel's causal incrementality with randomised holdouts.
The paid and organic last-click model ignores direct traffic.
Changing the model also changes user- and session-scoped dimensions such as Session source.
Changing the attribution model applies to historical as well as future data.
questions.explanation: Google Analytics Help says last click ignores direct traffic and that a model change applies to historical and future data. The change affects only event-scoped traffic dimensions; user- and session-scoped dimensions are unchanged. Data-driven attribution distributes credit from observed data and is not an experiment.
rationales: Data-driven is a credit-allocation model, not a randomised test.
Correct: last click ignores direct traffic.
User- and session-scoped dimensions are not affected.
Correct: the model change applies retroactively.

questions.scenario: A startup sells an AI document summariser to legal teams. Inference cost scales with pages processed, and the top 5% of users process 20 times more pages than the median user. Today the product is $25 per seat per month with unlimited use.
questions.stem: Which pricing change best aligns price with both customer value and cost to serve?
options: Move to a plan with an included page allowance per account, plus usage-based overage or credits beyond it
Keep unlimited per-seat pricing and raise the seat price for everyone until the blended margin is acceptable
Offer an unlimited free tier so heavy users self-select into a paid enterprise plan later
Charge a one-time licence fee so revenue does not depend on usage
questions.explanation: Pages processed is the unit that tracks both value and inference cost, so a hybrid plan with an allowance and overage protects margin while keeping a predictable base. A blanket seat increase overcharges light users and still leaves heavy users unprofitable.
rationales: Correct. An allowance plus overage ties price to the value metric that drives cost, while keeping bills predictable.
Raising every seat penalises light users and does not stop the heaviest users from costing more than they pay.
An unlimited free tier multiplies uncapped inference cost with no guaranteed path to revenue.
A one-time fee ignores ongoing inference costs entirely, so heavy users become permanently unprofitable.

questions.scenario: A team whiteboard app charges per seat. Analytics show many accounts share one login, and invites per account fell after a price rise. The product's growth depends on teammates joining boards.
questions.stem: What is the most likely pricing problem, and the best direction to fix it?
options: Login sharing is a security issue only; enforce single-device sessions and keep pricing as is
Switch to a free trial so customers have less time to share logins
The price level is too low; raise the seat price further to signal quality
The value metric suppresses adoption; make viewers or guests free and charge for editors or at account level
questions.explanation: Charging for every seat makes customers ration access in a collaborative product, which is exactly what shared logins and falling invites show. Free collaborator roles or an account-level metric keep the network effect while still charging for value.
rationales: Blocking sharing without fixing the incentive will push teams to invite fewer people or leave.
A trial changes the evaluation period, not the per-seat incentive to ration access after purchase.
A higher seat price would make rationing worse, not better.
Correct. The unit being charged is discouraging the behaviour that drives value; free collaborator roles or account-level pricing fix that.

questions.scenario: An AI coding assistant offers an unlimited free plan. Sign-ups are strong, but free users account for most inference spend and only a small share ever upgrade. The product's value is usually obvious within the first few days.
questions.stem: Which change is most appropriate?
options: Replace or cap the free plan with a time-limited trial or a small usage allowance, and track the free cohort's inference cost alongside conversion
Remove all free access and require a paid annual contract before first use
Keep unlimited free access but switch to a cheaper model only for paying users
Keep the unlimited free plan and add more paid features to the top tier
questions.explanation: Freemium works when free users are cheap to serve; here each free request costs inference money and value shows quickly, which favours a trial or a capped allowance. Measuring the free cohort's cost alongside conversion shows whether the funnel pays for itself.
rationales: Correct. Fast time-to-value and high marginal cost favour a time-limited trial or capped free usage, measured on cost as well as conversion.
Removing all free access is an over-correction that blocks evaluation when value shows quickly.
Downgrading paying users while giving free users the best model inverts the incentive to upgrade.
Adding paid features does nothing about uncapped free inference spend.

questions.scenario: A team is starting a brand-new Stripe integration to bill customers per API call with tiered overage. A developer proposes building it on the Meters API because an older tutorial uses it.
questions.stem: What does Stripe's current documentation recommend?
options: Use legacy usage records, because they are the only option that supports tiers
Use Metronome as the starting point for new usage-based integrations; the Meters API remains supported for existing integrations
Avoid Stripe for usage-based billing because it only supports fixed-price subscriptions
Use the Meters API, because Metronome is only for existing customers being migrated
questions.explanation: Stripe's usage-based billing docs describe Metronome (now part of Stripe) as the primary usage-based billing platform and the recommended starting point for new integrations, while the Meters API stays supported. Older tutorials predate this guidance.
rationales: Legacy usage records are kept in separate legacy docs and are not the recommended path for new work.
Correct. This matches Stripe's current guidance for new usage-based integrations.
Stripe supports usage-based billing; this claim is false.
This reverses the guidance: the Meters API is the one kept for existing integrations.

sources.title: Metronome vs Meters API — Stripe Docs

questions.scenario: An AI meeting-notes product charges $40 per account per month. On average each account drives $14 of model inference, $3 of production hosting and $1 of transcription API fees. Marketing spend is $9 per account per month on average.
questions.stem: What is the gross margin?
questions.explanation: COGS is the cost of delivering the product: 14 + 3 + 1 = $18, so gross margin = (40 − 18) / 40 = 55%. Marketing spend is an acquisition cost, not COGS, so it does not belong in the calculation.
rationales: 32.5% treats the $9 of marketing as COGS; marketing is an acquisition cost that belongs in CAC.
57.5% leaves out the $1 transcription API fee, which is a per-customer delivery cost.
65% counts only inference ($14) and leaves out hosting and the transcription API, which are also delivery costs.

questions.scenario: A B2B SaaS product has a blended CAC of $900. Average revenue per account is $75 per month and gross margin is 75%.
questions.stem: What is the CAC payback period?
options: 16 months
9 months
20 months
12 months
questions.explanation: CAC payback = CAC / (monthly revenue × gross margin) = 900 / (75 × 0.75) = 900 / 56.25 = 16 months. Using revenue without the margin adjustment would give an overly optimistic 12 months.
rationales: Correct. 900 / 56.25 = 16 months.
9 months has no basis in the formula; it understates the period.
20 months would correspond to a 60% margin, not the stated 75%.
12 months divides by revenue (900 / 75) and forgets that only gross margin repays acquisition cost.

questions.scenario: A subscription product has ARPA of $60 per month, 70% gross margin, 2% monthly churn and a CAC of $700. A founder reports LTV:CAC as 4.3:1 using LTV = ARPA / churn.
questions.stem: What is the gross-margin-adjusted LTV:CAC using the simple LTV formula, and what was wrong with the founder's figure?
options: 6:1; the founder should have divided by churn twice to account for compounding
4.3:1; the founder's figure is correct because LTV is defined on revenue
3:1; the founder used revenue instead of gross margin, which overstates LTV
2.1:1; the founder should have used annual churn instead of monthly churn
questions.explanation: Simple LTV = ARPA × gross margin / monthly churn = 60 × 0.7 / 0.02 = $2,100, and 2,100 / 700 = 3:1. The founder's 60 / 0.02 = $3,000 ignores delivery costs, which overstates LTV and the ratio.
rationales: Dividing by churn twice has no basis and grossly inflates LTV.
