Revenue-based LTV ignores the cost of delivering the product and overstates value, especially for AI products.
Correct. 60 × 0.7 / 0.02 = 2,100; 2,100 / 700 = 3:1. Leaving out margin inflates LTV.
Mixing annual churn with monthly ARPA breaks the unit consistency of the formula.

questions.scenario: For the customers active on 1 January, starting MRR was $200k. During the quarter, cancellations removed $10k, downgrades removed $6k and upgrades added $26k. New customers signed in the quarter added $40k.
questions.stem: What are NRR and GRR for the quarter?
options: NRR 105%, GRR 105%
NRR 113%, GRR 95%
NRR 125%, GRR 92%
NRR 105%, GRR 92%
questions.explanation: NRR = (200 − 10 − 6 + 26) / 200 = 105% and GRR = (200 − 10 − 6) / 200 = 92%. New-customer MRR is not part of either metric, and GRR excludes expansion.
rationales: GRR cannot include expansion, so it cannot equal NRR here.
95% leaves contraction out of GRR ((200 − 10) / 200), and 113% does not follow from the cohort's churn, contraction and expansion.
125% adds the $40k of new customers to NRR, which only measures the starting cohort.

questions.scenario: A board deck reports: "Gross revenue retention 108%, net revenue retention 115%, driven by strong seat expansion."
questions.stem: What is wrong with this report?
options: Nothing; strong expansion can push both GRR and NRR above 100%
GRR excludes expansion, so it cannot exceed 100%; the 108% figure must be miscalculated
NRR can never exceed GRR, so the two numbers are swapped
Seat expansion counts as new revenue and should be excluded from NRR
questions.explanation: GRR only subtracts churn and contraction from starting MRR and never adds expansion, so its maximum is 100%. NRR is the metric that includes expansion and can exceed 100%.
rationales: Expansion raises NRR only; GRR ignores it by definition.
Correct. GRR is capped at 100% because expansion is excluded.
NRR is always at least GRR because it adds expansion; it can and often does exceed GRR.
Expansion from existing customers is exactly what NRR is designed to include.

questions.scenario: Last quarter a SaaS company lost 12% of its customers, almost all on the cheapest plan. MRR lost to cancellations was 2% of starting MRR, and its three largest accounts doubled their seats. The CEO is alarmed by the 12%.
questions.stem: Which reading of the data is most accurate?
options: Logo churn is high but revenue churn is low and expansion is strong, so look at GRR and NRR for revenue health and investigate small-plan churn separately
Logo churn does not matter for SaaS and should be dropped from reporting
The company should combine logo and revenue churn into one average to resolve the conflict
Revenue health is collapsing; logo churn of 12% means NRR must be well below 100%
questions.explanation: Logo churn counts customers while revenue churn and NRR weight by MRR, so losing many small customers can coexist with healthy revenue retention. Both views matter: revenue metrics for financial health, logo churn for a possible problem in the low-end segment.
rationales: Correct. Read revenue health from GRR and NRR, and treat small-plan logo churn as a separate segment problem.
Logo churn still signals product-fit or onboarding problems in a segment; dropping it hides that.
Averaging two differently weighted metrics produces a number with no clear meaning.
Logo churn does not determine NRR; small-plan losses and large expansion can leave NRR above 100%.

questions.scenario: A finance analyst is computing gross margin for an AI support-chat product and has a list of monthly costs.
questions.stem: Which two costs belong in cost of goods sold for the gross-margin calculation? (Select two.)
options: Salaries of engineers building next quarter's new features
Model inference spend for answering customer chats
Paid search advertising to acquire new customers
Production hosting for the chat service and vector database
questions.explanation: COGS is what it costs to deliver the product to existing customers, so inference and production hosting belong there. Advertising is an acquisition cost that goes into CAC, and new-feature engineering is R&D.
rationales: Building future features is R&D (operating expense), not a cost of delivering today's product.
Correct. Inference is a direct, per-use cost of delivering an AI product.
Advertising is a sales and marketing cost; it belongs in CAC, not COGS.
Correct. Production infrastructure is a cost of delivering the service.

questions.scenario: A customer upgrades from a $10 to a $20 monthly plan exactly halfway through the billing period. Product wants the customer charged for the difference right away, not on next month's invoice.
questions.stem: How should the subscription update be configured on Stripe, and what net amount results?
options: proration_behavior: none; the customer is charged $20 immediately
proration_behavior: create_prorations; $5 is charged immediately
proration_behavior: always_invoice; a net $5 (−$5 credit, +$10 charge) is invoiced immediately
proration_behavior: always_invoice; a net $10 is invoiced immediately
questions.explanation: With always_invoice, Stripe creates the prorations and invoices them immediately; at the halfway point that is a −$5 credit for unused time on $10 and +$10 for half a period on $20, a net $5. create_prorations, the default, puts those items on the next invoice instead.
rationales: none creates no prorations at all, so no mid-period charge for the difference is made.
create_prorations is the default and adds the items to the next invoice rather than charging now.
Correct. always_invoice bills the prorations immediately, and the net is +$5.
$10 ignores the credit for the unused half of the $10 plan.

questions.scenario: A plan-change screen shows "You will be charged $X today" before the customer confirms. The amount is currently computed in the app's own code, and support tickets report that the final invoice sometimes differs by a few cents.
questions.stem: What is the most reliable fix?
options: Preview the change with invoices.create_preview using a fixed proration_date, show that amount, and pass the same proration_date when updating the subscription
Set proration_behavior to none so there is never a difference to explain
Compute prorations by whole days instead of seconds in the app so the numbers are simpler
Round the app's estimate to the nearest dollar and label it approximate
questions.explanation: Stripe computes prorations to the second, so an estimate made at one time and applied later drifts. Previewing with invoices.create_preview and reusing the same proration_date makes the shown amount match what Stripe bills.
rationales: Correct. A preview with a pinned proration_date, reused on the update, gives the exact amount.
Turning off prorations changes the business policy to dodge a display bug.
Stripe's own calculation is what bills the customer; a different method in the app guarantees mismatches.
Rounding hides the mismatch without fixing it and still leads to surprises on the invoice.

questions.scenario: A customer downgrades mid-period from a $50 plan to a $20 plan. The subscription uses the default proration behaviour. A week later they complain that no refund arrived.
questions.stem: What explains this, and what should the team do?
options: Downgrades are never prorated on Stripe, so no credit exists
The credit was lost because usage-based prices were involved
A bug: Stripe always refunds negative prorations to the card automatically
Negative prorations are not refunded automatically; they remain as credit, so issue a refund explicitly if the policy promises one
questions.explanation: Stripe's prorations docs state that negative prorations are not refunded automatically. If the business promises refunds on downgrade, the team must issue them explicitly; otherwise the credit offsets future invoices.
rationales: Downgrades do create prorations under the default create_prorations behaviour.
These are fixed-price plans. Usage-based prices are not prorated, but that does not explain a missing refund on a fixed-price downgrade.
Stripe does not automatically refund negative prorations.
Correct. The credit exists but is not refunded unless you refund it.

questions.scenario: A three-person team sells a downloadable design plugin to customers in dozens of countries. They have no tax staff and do not want to register for VAT and GST in each country. They sell through Stripe Checkout.
questions.stem: Which approach best fits, and what is the main trade-off?
options: Sell direct with Stripe Billing and ignore indirect tax until revenue is large
Use a merchant of record such as Stripe Managed Payments, accepting a fee on top of standard processing and less control (the sale is shown as through Link)
Use a merchant of record, which has no extra cost because tax savings cover the fee
Sell direct, because a merchant of record cannot be used with Checkout
questions.explanation: A merchant of record becomes the legal seller and handles indirect tax compliance, which suits a small team selling digital products globally. Stripe's Managed Payments works with Checkout, charges a fee on top of processing and presents the sale as sold through Link.
rationales: Ignoring indirect tax obligations creates liability; it is not a strategy.
Correct. An MoR removes the tax compliance burden in exchange for an extra fee and some loss of control.
Managed Payments charges a fee on top of standard processing; it is not free.
Managed Payments works through Checkout or Payment Links, so Checkout is not a blocker.

questions.scenario: A marketplace built on Stripe Connect lets independent makers sell physical craft kits. The team asks whether to move to Stripe Managed Payments to offload sales tax.
questions.stem: Which two facts make Managed Payments a poor fit here? (Select two.)
options: Managed Payments does not handle any indirect tax
Managed Payments does not support Connect
Managed Payments only works with Stripe Billing subscriptions, not one-off sales
Managed Payments supports only digital products
questions.explanation: Stripe's Managed Payments docs limit it to digital products and to direct integrations (no Connect platforms), so a Connect marketplace for physical goods fails on both counts. It does handle indirect tax, which is its main purpose, and it works through Checkout or Payment Links.
rationales: Handling indirect tax as merchant of record is the core purpose of Managed Payments.
Correct. Connect is not supported, which rules out this marketplace architecture.
Managed Payments is used through Checkout or Payment Links; it is not limited to Billing subscriptions.
Correct. It supports only digital products; physical goods such as craft kits are excluded.

questions.scenario: A SaaS company will raise its Pro plan from $30 to $36 per month for existing subscribers. Leadership wants to limit churn and support load.
questions.stem: Which two practices are the most responsible way to roll this out? (Select two.)
options: Change the existing price immediately and invoice everyone the $6 difference for the current period
Apply the increase silently and only explain if customers contact support
Give clear advance notice explaining what changes and when
Apply the new price at each customer's next renewal (or after a grandfather period) using a new Price
questions.explanation: A price increase for existing customers is a trust event, so advance notice and moving subscriptions to a new Price at renewal or after a grandfather period limit surprise and churn. Immediate mid-cycle charges and silent increases trigger disputes and cancellations.
rationales: An immediate charge for the current period surprises customers and invites chargebacks.
Silent increases damage trust and create disputes once customers notice.
Correct. Advance notice with a clear explanation reduces surprise and support load.
Correct. Switching at renewal or after a grandfather period avoids mid-cycle surprises.

questions.scenario: A team wants to test $20 vs $28 for its Team plan. The first design assigns a variant at random on each pricing-page view and declares the winner by checkout conversion after one week. Customers are companies, and several people from each company often visit the pricing page.
questions.stem: Which redesign is most responsible and most likely to give a valid answer?
options: Assign the variant with a stable hash of the account (group) key so everyone at a company sees one price, honour the price shown at purchase, and judge by revenue per visitor over a window that includes renewals and early churn
Show the lower price to returning visitors and the higher price to new ones, then compare conversion
Judge by click-through on the Buy button so the test finishes faster
Keep per-view randomisation but run it for two weeks instead of one
questions.explanation: Per-view randomisation lets the same buyer or colleagues see different prices, which damages trust and contaminates the comparison. Stable account-level bucketing, honouring shown prices and a revenue metric over a longer window measure the real trade-off between conversion and price.
rationales: Correct. Stable group bucketing, honoured prices and revenue over a longer window make the test fair and valid.
Splitting by new vs returning visitors confounds the price with visitor intent.
Button clicks are an even weaker proxy than conversion and ignore revenue and churn.
A longer run does not fix people within one company seeing different prices.
